item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: whether colourfully anodised or powder-coated, or left in a brown- or silver-toned state, the following products are all made from metals.

The selection includes tables, storage, seating and lighting all made from stainless steel, aluminium or steel.

Metal is often selected by designers thanks to its practical and aesthetic properties. It is durable while being at once both timeless and futuristic.

Read on to discover a selection of metallic furnishings from design brands based the world over, from Belgium to South Korea.

Miro side table by Candour Antwerp

A trio of stainless steel pieces comprises this side table by design brand Candour Antwerp, which can be disassembled and alternatively used separately as a vase and mirror.

Miro's body is finished in a more matte way, while its tabletop is mirror polished. Despite this and its three possible functions, its materiality lends it one consistent aesthetic.

Find out more about Miro ›

Stack furniture system by Studio Moto

Aluminium gives this modular storage system by Belgian architecture practice Studio Moto both visual consistency and practical benefits.

The Stack furniture system can be taken apart and put back together using its interlocking system, through which users can create shelving and tables at will.

Find out more about Stack ›

Scaffold outdoor occasional tables by Haldane

Round-ended lengths of stainless steel replace bamboo in this Japanese scaffolding-informed series of tables by South African designer Haldane Martin.

Scaffold outdoor occasional tables come in polished stainless steel or in one of thirty powder-coated colourways.

Find out more about Scaffold ›

Linde chair by OUT

German design brand OUT's Linde chair – a dining seat with the "comfort of an armchair" – is supported by metal legs configured into a range of bases.

Available in four-legged or swivel base options, the legs are made from either polished stainless steel or polished aluminium in either silver or powder-coated colourways.

Find out more about Linde ›

Filosof lamp by Lars-Erik Ejlers and Fripon

Originally created by architect Lars-Erik Ejlers in 1990 for a Copenhagen restaurant, the Filosof pendant has been reissued by Danish company Fripon.

Traditional metal spinning processes are employed to create the fitting, which comprises three concentric shades: one brass, one copper and one black anodised aluminium.

Find out more about Filosof ›

Domus outdoor lighting collection by Joan Gaspar for Marset

Designer Joan Gaspar looked to the appearance of houses illuminated at night when creating the Domus outdoor lighting collection for Spanish brand Marset.

The lights' angular housing is made from steel and aluminium, chosen for their ability to withstand the elements, and comes in a trio of colourways including rust brown.

Find out more about Domus ›

DOB Modular System by Flat Point

Block colour cabinet fronts meet metal housing in this storage system by South Korean brand Flat Point.

The DOB Modular System is aluminium-made and stands for "disassemble or build", owing to its flexibility.

Find out more about DOB Modular System ›

Hangman lighting collection by Adam Goodrum for Rakumba

Specially-engineered joints that allow repositioning characterise this deceptively simple series of lights by Australian designer Adam Goodrum for design brand Rakumba.

The Hangman lighting collection comes in polished, powder-coated or anodised aluminium finishes, some of which are limited editions.

Find out more about Hangman ›

item.content:encoded:
A series of cascading terraces outline the North Tower skyscraper by architecture studio SOM, which has topped out on a waterfront site in Chicago.

Rising 261 metres at the confluence of Lake Michigan and the Chicago River, the North Tower's recently-completed concrete and steel structure features a stepped silhouette cloaked in glass and topped with a 25-metre-tall crown.

Slated for completion in 2027, the North Tower is the first of two residential skyscrapers being built as part of SOM's ongoing 400 Lake Shore Drive development. Construction is yet to begin on the neighbouring South Tower.

The North Tower's glass-covered facade, which tapers towards its top, was designed by SOM as nod to traditional Chicago bay windows, complete with metal detailing that draws on the "movement of Lake Michigan".

Behind this, the tower's mechanical systems and maintenance unit have been concealed within the structural frame to establish a "clean, uninterrupted" exterior profile.

Read:

World's tallest timber tower tops out in Sydney

"The building's facade reinterprets the Chicago bay window for a contemporary high-rise, using a faceted glass curtain wall to bring depth, rhythm, and texture to the tower's exterior," the studio said.

"The geometry of the facade opens views from the residences while giving the building a shifting, reflective quality that responds to changing light and weather along the lakefront," it added.

Once it has been fitted out, the North Tower will contain 635 residences, including 127 affordable apartments. Meanwhile, at ground level, a plaza will provide public amenities for both residents and visitors.

"When complete, 400 Lake Shore Drive will form a new gateway to downtown Chicago from the lakefront," the studio said.

"The North and South Towers are angled in relation to one another to preserve view corridors and create a unique presence at the edge of Streeterville."

Elsewhere, the world's tallest timber tower designed by SHoP Architects and BVN Architecture has topped out in Sydney and Studio Libeskind has designed a cluster of Seoul skyscrapers as "a living work of art".

The photography is by Dave Burk courtesy of SOM.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: design brand OUT has released a Berlin-made chair and table set that aims to enhance the comfort and functionality of dining spaces.

Berlin-based brand OUT – whose unabbreviated name is Objekte Unserer Tage – describes the Linde chair as having the "comfort of an armchair, brought to the dining table".

Each of its elements can be switched out to extend the piece's lifespan. Users are also able to select from various base options and two upholstery styles – one smooth and one with a draped aesthetic named Linde Soft.

"At the beginning, there was the image of a blossoming flower," said OUTS's head of design David Wendt. "A form that opens, feels present, yet carries something very soft – I wanted to translate exactly that feeling into the chair."

As well as having a monolithic and statuesque aesthetic, the Linde table's thick cylindrical base and underside of the wooden tabletop double as an acoustic product thanks to their upholstered nature, which also results in a perfectly smooth surface broken up by chic seams.

"The seams are set into precisely milled channels, with a level of craftsmanship typically found in the interior of a luxury automobile," said OUT. "This is where the technique comes from. Above, the tabletop in solid ash wood sits like a macaron, guiding the hand softly along its edge."

Both pieces are designed in Berlin and made in Germany.

item.content:encoded:
Slovakian studio Cechvala Architects has completed RDH, a contemporary family home in Bratislava composed of three stacked volumes clad in corrugated aluminium.

Situated next to a horticultural centre in Bratislava's Sihot district, the three-storey house sits between a branch of the Danube River and the foothills of the Carpathian mountains.

RDH's three stacked volumes include a more solid base supporting a glazed first floor and a smaller upper volume that opens out onto a roof terrace.

This design was partly shaped by an existing building permit issued in 2009, which Cechvala Architects said determined the footprint, height and position on the site.

It also aims to balance the client's desire for privacy with connection to the surrounding landscape.

The elevations facing the neighbouring properties are largely solid, while those overlooking the river open up with expansive glazing.

Read:

Nick Kent Design designs Bondi House as steel-framed "kit of parts"

Due to its location within a flood zone, the studio opted for a durable material palette, using untreated corrugated aluminium to clad the exterior.

"The raw aluminium facade absorbs the light and colour of its surroundings, changing and adapting throughout the day," Cechvala Architects' Ondrej Zajac told Dezeen.

Entry is on the ground floor, which contains a garage, fitness area and utility spaces. At the centre of the plan, a dark steel staircase zigzags through a full-height concrete stairwell, with a skylight above drawing natural light deep into the interior.

Thin vertical steel balustrades allow views through the slender staircase, while a cylindrical black woodburner echoes its dark finish.

The first floor contains the home's open-plan living space and bedroom, where exposed concrete ceilings are paired with pale timber flooring and built-in furniture pieces.

According to the studio, the house was organised around a modular structural grid that allows internal partitions to be reconfigured over time.

"Due to the placement of the columns and the position of the staircase, occupants could change the location of rooms without requiring any major structural interventions," said Zajac.

"The essential message of the design is that the house can age together with its occupant, adapting to their life almost on the fly," Zajac stated.

Full-height glazing opens the living spaces and bedroom onto terraces overlooking the river and surrounding landscape.

Cantilevered terraces were designed to provide passive solar shading during the summer months while allowing lower winter sun to warm the interior. Textile screens around the terraces can also be lowered when needed to provide additional shade and privacy.

Other Slovakian homes featured on Dezeen include an apartment for artists by Alan Prekop Studio that occupies a former office and a Y-shaped house by Paulíny Hovorka Architects surrounded by a rock garden.

The photography is by Alex Shoots Buildings.

item.content:encoded:
London biotech company CipherX has created the world's first commercially available microdot tattoo, which is applied using a pain-free applicator.

Launched yesterday, the permanent tattoos are created using dissolvable microneedles instead of a traditional tattoo gun. This means that the application is a pain-free process.

"You end up with the same permanent tattoo, and I should really stress that," CipherX co-founder Ferdinand Kohle. "The result is the same, but the application process is completely different."

So far CipherX has applied 500 microdot tattoos, and following its launch in London, it is now available commercially for the first time.

Described by CipherX as "a fundamentally new way of tattooing", the tattoo is applied from a patch that contains numerous microneedles made of a combination of tattoo ink and a polymer.

This patch is rammed onto the skin using an applicator that pushes the ink-based microneedles into the skin, which dissolve to create the permanent tattoo. The patch is left on the skin for 15 minutes then removed, with no aftercare required.

Kohle, a material scientist who gained his PhD from Cornell, developed the idea for the painless tattoos after initially planning to set up a company to develop microneedles to administer pharmaceuticals.

"I was working with injections, so it was injection devices, syringes, auto injectors, et cetera," explained Kohle. "That was my day-to-day, but I hate needles; it's like a true phobia – I get cold sweat even thinking about them."

Read:

Blackdot's AI-powered tattoo device promises to make tattoos faster and less painful

"So I was working with needles, which I thought was a little ironic, and I was always interested in entrepreneurship so I thought, okay, I am going to start a company," he continued.

"So I came to London with the idea of starting another company, when suddenly I had the idea that you could use micro needle technology to deliver tattoos – deliver pigment."

Due to the size of the ink-based microneedles, they do not penetrate as deeply into the skin as traditional tattoo needles, which makes the process painless.

"Communicating the scale is actually a very challenging topic," said Kohle. "People have a mental image of a needle, they think immediately of the needle used for injections."

"But you can scale it down, and that changes its properties and how you interact with it," he continued. "When you scale the needle down and you apply it to your skin, you don't really feel the penetration anymore because it doesn't actually touch your pain receptors."

Kohle hopes that his process will allow people who have previously been afraid or unable to get tattoos to get them.

"When I was like 18 or 19, I really wanted to get a tattoo, but I was a little scared, and then I never really did it," he said. "So actually this is really cool for people like me."

However, he is keen to express that he does not think that the microdot tattoos will replace traditional tattoos.

"We are in no means trying to replace any tattoo artists – I don't even think that would be possible," said Kohle.

"If you ask me, what is the target customer? One of the target groups is people like myself who would just not get a regular tattoo, and in fact, it has already been proven to be very attractive to these people."

CipherX's microdot tattoos are currently available in a limited number of designs that range in size from 3 to 11 millimetres.

Kohle is now planning to expand the range with customisation planned in the future. CipherX is also exploring medical applications and has received several grants from Innovate UK to further develop this application.

In other tattoo news, last year Blackdot developed an AI-powered tattoo device that it says is faster, safer, and less painful than a human-made tattoo.

The photography is by CipherX unless stated.

item.content:encoded:
A curved brick structure by architecture studio SANAA has been selected as the new design for the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, following reports that locals had criticised the original winning design.

Set to be built along the border of La Carolina Park in Quito near projects by studios such as BIG, Kengo Kuma and Safdie Architects, the winning design for the Museo Nacional de Ecuador is imagined as "a system of interconnected vertical plazas" wrapped in terracotta brick.

The project team includes SANAA in collaboration with Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0, Jerome Haferd Studio and Taller Capital Landscape. It refers to itself as SANAA + A0-CPA-JHS.

Named Living Strata, its selection follows the Ecuadorian government's recall of a blocky design by Spanish practice Studio Alberto Campo Baeza and local studio MAODA earlier this month after an online petition criticising the design drew thousands of signatures by disgruntled citizens.

The new scheme originally came in third place in a competition for the project. After the original 10 finalists resubmitted designs following the public backlash, it was announced as the winner on 19 July, according to reports.

Its design draws on "pre-Columbian and post-Columbian cultures" and aims to "reflect all Ecuadorian people", according to the team.

The building will comprise nine storeys, including storage and parking floors below ground, and have several circular openings that bore through the main volume to create courtyards.

Circular pools and planting beds will also surround the building's plaza.

Read:

National Museum of Ecuador recalls Alberto Campo Baeza design after public backlash

"Inspired by pre-Columbian and post-Columbian cultures, the project embraces the circle as an expression of collective memory, gathering, and connection with the cosmos," said the team.

"The project aims to reflect all Ecuadorian people and invites the international community to engage in the rich history."

Galleries will be located on the upper floors, while the lower plaza level is designed to become an extension of La Carolina Park, according to the team.

The museum's curvilinear form will also aim to "establish a dialogue with the Pichincha volcano", which overlooks Quito.

The National Museum of Ecuador's groundbreaking is anticipated for 2027.

The museum has gone through several iterations under different names since the late 1960s. This most recent project, catalysed under Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, aims to establish a new and permanent home for the museum, which is primarily programmed around local art and culture.

While the team acknowledged that the proposal was "ultimately selected as part of a finalist phase that included a jury assessment and a public Ecuadorian voting process", it told Dezeen it has no further comments on the competition's outcome at this time.

In response to the original design being recalled, its architects Campo Baeza and MAODA said they had been locked out of a public debate, citing how this process led to landmark projects such as Sydney Opera House and Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao.

"[Those projects] were enriched by this debate and are today part of the landscape and the immemorial heritage of those cities," read their statement.

Other projects recently completed around the broader area of La Carolina Park include the EPIQ tower by BIG and a skyscraper made of stacked units by Safdie Architects.

The images are courtesy of SANAA + A0-CPA-JHS.

item.content:encoded:
Tech company Light has released a clamshell version of its popular minimalist phone, combining contemporary dumbphone functionality with retro appeal.

A follow-up to 2025's all-black Light Phone 3, the Light Flip comes in six colours and runs Light's intentionally stripped-back LightOS operating system, which is devoid of social media, games and other common distractions.

Light said the new device with its clamshell-style design responded to the resurgence of interest in flip phones, which have become particularly popular among members of Generations Z and Alpha.

"Time and time again, we've heard from people – especially the younger generations – who love flip phones, but the current options are poorly made, slow, unsupported and often pre-installed with the same addictive apps built in," the company said.

"Light is taking everything that already works for tens of thousands of Light Phone users and is bringing that into a heavily desired yet timeless tactile form factor of a flip phone."

The flip phone form factor "prioritises calling, a far superior way to catch up, make plans or celebrate" and lets users "experience the distinct satisfaction of hanging up", Light added.

The Light Flip otherwise continues Light's design philosophy of creating technology that is designed to be used as little as possible.

It includes a matt 2.8-inch screen for viewing the company's entirely black-and-white, text-based OS, with an editable selection of apps including a calendar, alarm, calculator, maps, podcasts, weather, notes, voice memos and an authenticator tool.

There is also a music app, but it is for music files rather than streaming services, and a 12-megapixel rear camera with a 50-megapixel sensor, but no front "selfie" camera.

There are some divergences from the Light Phone 3. The Light Flip does not have the more premium phone's AMOLED screen, instead featuring OLED, and instead of the aluminium and glass body, it is made from plastic. The Light Flip is also less than half the price of the Light Phone 3, at US$299 (£225).

Other elements that may appeal to fans of retro technology are the numeric keypad with predictive T9 texting and the ability to put nine contacts on speed dial.

Read:

Four of the best dumbphones for a digital detox

The modern conveniences of USB-C, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, 5G connectivity and audio and voice-to-text messaging are all included.

New apps may soon become available through Light's recently launched developer programme, which it hopes will lead to the creation of a curated, non-commercial, open-source platform where users can download additional tools in lieu of an app store.

However, the company stresses that there are some features the phones will never have: social media, internet browsing, email, news, ads or infinite feeds.

"As Apple, Google, and others race to build AI deeper into everything, despite growing backlash from consumers, Light is making the case for a radically different future," said the company.

The Light Flip has been designed for repair and includes a user-replaceable battery, the company added.

It is available in red, pink, yellow, navy, grey and black and is shipping from April 2027.

Light was one of the first companies to launch a contemporary dumbphone or brickphone, combining new technologies with intentional limitations, when it released the first Light Phone in 2017.

Its most recent version, the Light Phone 3, was the highest-scoring device in Dezeen's dumbphone road test, thanks to its calming screen experience and well-thought-out feature set.

item.content:encoded:
In this week's comments update, readers are discussing MVRDV's winning proposal for social enterprise Shift's competition to design a €240 million landmark in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.

Named Rotterdam Rocks!, the project, which was designed to resemble stacked rocks with terraces and greenery, was the most radical of the five submissions.

"Actual nature does it better"

Commenters were largely on the same page.

"Horror!" wrote Fokkovanderveen. "A terrible nightmare!".

Ozspur, meanwhile, wrote "Looks like something Shrek would throw up."

"Just when it felt Rotterdam was starting to grow up, this comes along," said Will, exasperated. "I'm embarrassed for a wonderful city."

In agreement, Alfred Hitchcock said, "It doesn't look 'wonderful'. It's the Marble Arch Mound regurgitated and remodelled, and we know how well that went."

"Is this the death certificate of architecture?" Vinny asked.

In terms of its ecological stance, Ramsey Jansen said, "There is nothing 'green' about this monstrosity. Just a facade wearing a costume, with a maintenance bill nobody's talking about yet."

"Actual nature does it better," wrote Name Changer.

Though, amongst the slew of negativity, one commenter was impressed by the project.

"Love this," said HP. "It's an original design and could be wonderful."

What do you think? Join the discussion ›

"Are we now fully living in The Simpsons' world?"

Another story with an inundated comment section was the approval of a giant space mirror by the US federal government, intended to illuminate parts of the Earth at night.

"Humanity is cooked in more ways than one!" exclaimed Paul Wilcox.

Concurring, Dave wrote, "Humans will get so smart we will destroy ourselves, all in the name of science."

Monte said, "In order to solve one problem, we create a hundred others." To this, Imenda replied, "I would also not call night and darkness a problem."

"It just gets sillier everyday," said Bloibl, while Whateverandeverman wrote, "Checks calendar… not April 1st."

"Are we now fully living in The Simpsons' world?" asked Chris W, while Zmorg dubbed it a "tech-bro Death Star."

"I think the best thing to do would be to take this idea and stuff it where the sun don't shine," agreed Charlie Bing unenthusiastically.

"My day ruined," wrote Chauncey Mabe. "And your night," joked Stephano in response.

Have you had your say yet? Join the discussion ›

"Race you to the top"

One project that received a round of applause was KPF's design of tech company TP-Link's offices in Shenzhen, China, which are wrapped in a one-kilometre-long sequence of terraces and planted staircases.

"Back in the day, KPF would once in a while belt out a gem that rose above their standard corporate flair, and this seems like another one," wrote Heywood Floyd. "Very inventive use of that exterior space, and the exterior massing is quite interesting."

H T Holman agreed, writing, "A fascinating use of the exterior space."

"Interesting ideas," said Pa Varreon. "Clean and quiet architecture."

Just as impressed, MKE Tom wrote, "Beautiful design and use of the exterior ribbon of space. It is both simultaneously an intimate and grand gesture."

"This feels like actual landscaping," said MrG. "Plants are often just slapped on to make an otherwise boring building look nice in the renderings."

"Race you to the top," wrote Design Junkie.

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion ›

Keep up to date on the latest discussions on our comments page and subscribe to our weekly Debate newsletter, where we feature the best reader comments from stories in the past seven days.

Architecture studio Red Deer sourced Gerolakkos stone and hand-crafted Lefkara lace from Cyprus, which it juxtaposed with stainless steel and oversized basket-like lamps at Zylia in Covent Garden.

The design of the restaurant, which serves food inspired by Greek Cypriot cooking, was adapted to suit the old factory building in which it's located and reference the provenance of its menu.

"We wanted to introduce a distinctly Cypriot sensibility into the existing shell, a former Victorian blacking factory in Covent Garden," Red Deer founding director Lionel Real de Azúa told Dezeen.

"The design became an exercise in dialogue rather than imitation, allowing materials, textures and references from Cyprus to inhabit an unmistakably London industrial building."

After a trip to Cyprus together with Zylia co-founder Barry Karacostas, Real de Azúa decided that the island country's Gerolakkos stone would be one of the features of the restaurant.

"One of the defining materials is Gerolakkos stone, or pouropetra, the warm honey-coloured limestone found throughout Cyprus and used for centuries in everything from civic buildings to humble garden walls," he said.

"The slabs used on the main counter and waiter stations were quarried and shipped directly from Cyprus, arriving only days before completion."

The tactile stone slabs were contrasted with stainless-steel finishes, which were used on the tabletops and chair legs.

"The contrast is important. Rather than allowing one material to dominate the other, the project relies on the tension between them," Real de Azúa said.

As well as the solid materials, Red Deer also drew on Cyprus' tradition of handcrafts when creating the interior, which features local lace and woven pendant lights that add a homely feel.

Read:

House of Baby designs Brixton restaurant Banh Banh as "immersive artwork"

"Traditional Lefkara lace, hand-crafted and brought from Cyprus, rests upon the stainless surfaces almost as an unexpected domestic intervention," Real de Azúa explained.

"The delicacy of the embroidery softens the precision of the metal, introducing a quiet humanity into what might otherwise feel overtly industrial."

The striking lamps that define the interior were a contemporary reinterpretation of traditional baskets found in Cyprus.

"Their intricate construction and tactile quality have a remarkable ability to make even the simplest interiors feel inhabited and warm," Real de Azúa said.

"Rather than reproducing these forms exactly, together with lighting designers Atelier Lighting, we enlarged and abstracted them, creating generous woven shades that hover above the central dining space," he continued.

"Their scale allows them to establish an architectural presence while retaining the intimacy associated with domestic craft."

For the colour palette of Zylia, Red Deer drew on "the muted greens of ageing timber shutters, their paint gently faded beneath decades of Mediterranean sunlight" in Nicosia, Cyprus.

These hues were then used for the upholstery and cushions in the space, complemented by the ochre colour of the Gerolakkos stone.

"The ambition was never to reproduce Cyprus literally, but to evoke its atmosphere through colour: a palette that feels sun-worn rather than fashionable, quietly confident rather than decorative," Real de Azúa concluded.

Other recent eateries that have opened in London include a popular southeast London bakery and a Vietnamese restaurant in Brixton with a modernist interior.

The photography is courtesy of Zylia.

Promotion: San Francisco and London-based start-up Avoice has created an AI agent designed to run the entire operational side of an architecture studio.

While much of the focus on artificial intelligence (AI) in the architecture profession is aimed at image generation, Avoice was designed to reduce the administrative load behind running a studio.

Avoice's platform is structured into three AI-powered products – Avoice Delivery, Avoice Projects, and Avoice Practice – each designed to solve distinct problems for mid-sized architectural practices.

Avoice Delivery focuses on how the practice delivers projects. Here, the AI agent handles anything from specification writing to drawing reviews, which eliminates the need for drawing specs from scratch.

"AI does the heavy lifting while the architect stays in control," explained Avoice.

Avoice Projects assists with tasks, to-do lists, project schedules and team coordination. The company explained that compared to project management tools such as Monday or Asana, Avoice Projects is directly connected to the project's delivery, so when a spec changes or an issue is flagged, tasks and schedules update automatically.

Finally, Avoice Practice focuses on how a "practice operates as a business". Here, the AI agent assists with project finances, invoicing, timesheets and studio-wide reporting.

"The AI conversation in our industry starts and ends with image generation," said Avoice co-founder Chawin Asavasaetakul. "Meanwhile, the actual work of delivering buildings hasn't been touched."

"Every professional function has AI agents handling operational work end-to-end – except architecture," he continued.

The product aims to be a single platform that can improve the specifications, QA/QC coordination, construction administration, project finances, client management, email, accounting and operations.

According to its creators, it replaces numerous individual systems currently being used in architecture studios with one coherent, AI-powered platform.

"None of them [individual systems] talk to each other," said Asavasaetakul. "When a specification changes, someone has to manually update the schedule, check the drawings, notify the consultant, and revise the budget. With Avoice, AI agents handle that chain automatically."

This single platform replaces the numerous different software products currently being used, which are not compatible with each other, meaning that processes are streamlined, giving architects more time to design.

"Architecture firms run on a patchwork of tools that don't talk to each other," said Asavasaetakul.

"An email lives in Gmail, he continued. "The spec lives in one tool. The schedule lives in a spreadsheet. QA markups live in a PDF. The budget lives somewhere else. Every time something changes, someone has to manually stitch it all together. Our agents do that automatically because everything lives in one place."

According to its creators, AI has reduced the cost of developing software, meaning that it is now economically viable to use one piece of consolidated software. This will ultimately improve the efficiency of running an architecture studio.

Based in San Francisco, the startup is backed by the accelerator Y Combinator, known for supporting companies such as Airbnb and Dropbox.

To find out more about Avoice, visit the company's website.

Dezeen School Shows: a theatre in London designed for international students, refugees, asylum seekers, early-career workers and first-generation migrants is among projects from Middlesex University.

Also featured is a charity-led music library and recording studio seeking to reduce youth crime and a civic-religious space aiming to counteract loneliness.

Middlesex University

Courses: BA (Hons) Interior Architecture, BA (Hons) Interior Design and MA Interiors (Architecture and Design)
Tutors: Rebecca Disney, Jason Scoot, Naomi House, Alex Tzortzis, Jon Mortimer, Michael Westthorp and Francesca Murialdo

School statement:

"At Middlesex University London, BA (Hons) Interior Architecture, BA (Hons) Interior Design and MA Interiors (Architecture and Design) students investigate the power of interiors to respond to the urgent challenges of our time, from climate responsibility and adaptive reuse to social inclusion and new ways of living, working and connecting.

"Working with existing buildings, communities and real-world contexts, students learn to see interiors as evolving spaces shaped by people, memory, culture and change.

"Through research-led design, experimentation and making, they develop proposals that question conventions and imagine more sustainable and meaningful futures.

"Our studio culture encourages collaboration, curiosity and individual voices. Students are supported to become critical designers who combine creative thinking with practical skills – from drawing, digital technologies and material exploration to storytelling and communication.

"The projects presented here celebrate the diversity of approaches within Middlesex Interiors: from intimate spatial experiences to larger questions of reuse, belonging and transformation.

"Together, they demonstrate how the next generation of designers can create spaces with purpose, responsibility and impact.

"Interior Architecture and Interior Design at Middlesex is a top-ten Guardian-ranked course, reaching as high as third in the UK.

"Strong NSS results highlight teaching quality, academic support and studio culture, while placements and career-focused learning prepare students to contribute creatively and responsibly across diverse sectors."

Discreet Communities: Between Permanence and Drift by Nicoleta Mereuta

"Winning the Progressing Students Award for Interior Educators Conference Award 2026, Discreet Communities: Between Permanence and Drift reimagines the London Canal Museum as a dynamic interior landscape shaped by seasonally controlled water levels.

"Responding to the spatial constraints and transitory nature of canal boat living, the project provides London's bargees community with a dedicated space for wellbeing and social connection.

"Drawing on the site's history of ice storage and canal infrastructure, the museum's historic ice wells are transformed into thermal environments that adapt throughout the year.

"In winter, the building becomes a sheltered retreat for yoga, bathing and communal gathering. In summer, flooded ice wells activate a floating spa that rises through the building, reconnecting occupants with the canal."

Student: Nicoleta Mereuta
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Architecture

The Care Exchange: Community-Led Social Infrastructure for Postnatal Care, Inclusion and Collective Wellbeing by Rachel Koh

"Rachel Koh's interior architecture project challenges the fragmentation and isolation experienced during postnatal care.

"The Care Exchange reframes care as a civic right, not a clinical afterthought, creating a community-embedded infrastructure for mothers, caregivers and families.

"Rejecting sterile healthcare environments, it proposes a hybrid hub where rest, healthcare, learning and social connection coexist.

"By weaving together support networks, intergenerational spaces and partnerships with local organisations, the project positions care as a collective social practice.

"It argues that meanwhile sites can reveal, and even repair, the social fractures that leave new parents unseen."

Student: Rachel Koh
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Architecture

Loneliness in Resonance: The Space That Listens by Jaden Siew

"Part of our live project, Practices of Reuse initiative, Jaden Siew's interior architecture proposal, developed with A Space for Us: The People's Museum in Somers Town, London, recasts St Mary's Church as a hybrid civic-religious space that confronts loneliness head-on.

"Through spatial mapping, sensory choreography and material provocation, she turns the church into an acoustic landscape where isolation becomes something you can hear, touch and move through.

"A tensile fabric-and-timber system stretches, slackens and shifts the interior, exposing voices, memories and shared traces. Visitors travel from Alone, In-between, Together and Return, encountering gentle connections without pressure."

Student: Jaden Siew
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Architecture

Lost Places: Homes – Architecture, Memory and the Aftermath of Displacement by Yui Shiroyama

"Yui Shiroyama's interior architecture writing journal examines what happens emotionally and architecturally when people lose their homes, tracing a three-part narrative through Pripyat, Torre David and Kiruna.

"Each case study reveals a different stage in the journey from displacement to reconstruction, showing how built form becomes a vessel for memory and identity.

"A participatory exercise asking 'What makes you feel at home?' produced a collective visual archive of personal objects, exposing shared values across diverse backgrounds.

"Together, the research positions architecture as an empathetic medium capable of helping displaced communities rebuild belonging."

Student: Yui Shiroyama
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Architecture

The Reference Room by Bridget Loftus

"A hybrid of theory and practice through material reference. The Reference Room reimagines interior design as a thoughtful, circular practice where public engagement, professional research and material reuse come together.

"Combining a sustainable homeware shop, café, exhibition space, reference library, materials archive, shared workspaces and designer-in-residence studio, the project invites visitors and designers to experience materials as both resource and story.

"Using reclaimed and natural materials, reversible construction and adaptable detailing, it reduces waste while celebrating texture, history and longevity.

"Rather than treating reuse as compromise, the project shows how responsible material choices can create richness, character and value, offering a timely model for sustainable, experiential design."

Student: Bridget Loftus
Course: BA Interior Design

Diffusing Social Barriers through Music by Bryony Johnson

"Sirlute's proposed central hub extends the charity's mission to reduce youth crime by widening access to the creative industries and supporting local talent.

"Centred on a music library, music-making spaces and recording studio, the project gives young people from under-resourced communities free access to mentoring, skills training and musical expression.

"It promotes inclusivity by bringing different social demographics together, creating a non-judgmental space where identity, confidence and life skills can develop through collaboration.

"Through social interaction, creative practice and shared experience, the hub supports mental well-being, strengthens community connection and empowers emerging youth culture."

Student: Bryony Johnson
Course: BA Interior Design

Between Presence by Arina Bielikova

"Soak is a thoughtful wellness environment that explores how openness, privacy and community can coexist in contemporary live-work culture.

"Sponsored by an international wellness brand, the three-storey space supports two recent graduates as they build professional confidence within the wellness industry, making their learning, dedication and daily rituals gently visible rather than hidden.

"A kinetic translucent façade, layered thresholds and filtered light create a carefully moderated relationship between residents and visitors, encouraging trust, connection and shared presence.

"Drawing on spa rituals, steam and soft bodily references, the project offers an intelligent, responsible model of care, where design nurtures people, careers and community."

Student: Arina Bielikova
Course: BA Interior Design

Theatre for Migrants by Migrants by Maria Balaban

"Theatre for Migrants by Migrants proposes a hybrid theatre studio and community venue where acting-based group classes become a practical tool for wellbeing, language confidence and belonging.

"Designed for new Londoners, including international students, refugees, asylum seekers, early-career workers and first-generation migrants, the project creates a consistent weekly 'third place' beyond school, therapy or nightlife.

"In a compact heritage setting, flexible performance, social and safeguarding spaces support playful collaboration, spoken English and low-pressure connection.

"Thoughtful, responsible design positions creative expression as a civic right, helping reduce isolation, build confidence and strengthen shared community identity across cultures in the city."

Student: Maria Balaban
Course: BA Interior Design

Group project: Phoenix Cinema

"MA and BA Interior students at Middlesex University collaborated on a live brief to redesign the foyer of East Finchley's Phoenix Cinema, a beloved art-house venue and one of the UK's oldest continuously running cinemas.

"Blending community insight with imaginative spatial thinking, student teams produced four distinct proposals celebrating the Phoenix's heritage while enhancing visitor experience.

"The client described them as 'four outstanding design proposals, each offering a unique vision for the future of the Phoenix'.

"The project gave students hands-on industry experience, culminating in the exciting prospect that one of their designs will be built and enjoyed by local audiences."

Students: Abyudh Gajja, Marco Leung, Alex Smith, Niloofar Toutounchi, Sharnagati Bhosale, Parisa Naserbakht, Hibah Sadiq, Glehan Segera, Ammarah Ismath, Joanne Lai, Bridget Loftus, Shaun Yow, Sava Alam, Yee Mon Aung, Methmi Dankoluwage, Tehreem Kashif and Nasrin Najafabadi
Course: MA Interiors

Open Frameworks by Methmi Dankoluwage

"Developed in our MA Interiors programme, the project frames Adaptive Reuse as a record of participation over a highly extended time period.

"The currently vacant Pentland commercial campus site, in North London, will evolve over many years. The existing structural frame remains, while new architectural interventions extend beyond the moment of design, responding to future needs.

"Rather than a fixed proposal, the project creates conditions for adaptation, repair and refinement, allowing users to become active authors through ongoing acts of use, maintenance, modification and collective engagement.

"By embracing incompletion as sustainable practice, Open Frameworks ensures the site can be utilised even in phases of disrepair, aligning with the programme's focus on adaptive reuse and radical sustainability."

Student: Methmi Dankoluwage
Course: MA Interiors

item.content:encoded:
US studio Manica has unveiled the design for a 70,000-seat stadium for the Kansas City Chiefs NFL team, which will be topped with a transparent dome.

The fully enclosed venue, which will replace the team's iconic Arrowhead Stadium, is set to cost $3 billion and open in 2031. According to Kansas City Chiefs CEO Clark Hunt, the stadium will be a modern venue that aims to replicate the feeling, noise and tailgating experience of the existing stadium.

"It's spectacular," said Hunt. "It honors the rich legacy of this franchise while setting a bold course for the future of Chiefs Kingdom."

"While we're still finalizing many of the details, there are a few things we know for sure: it will hold 70,000 fans, it will still be the best place in the world to tailgate, and the whole building will be built for noise," he continued.

Unlike Arrowhead Stadium, the venue will be topped with a translucent roof made of 37,000 square metres of EFTE panels designed to "maximize visibility for military flyovers".

While enclosed, the new stadium's shape evokes the current stadium, with the geometry and shape designed to create a noisy environment.

Key Arrowhead characteristics including the "drum deck" and a roll of honour around the top of the stadium will be incorporated into the design.

Bucking the trend for NFL teams to consider urban locations, the Kansas City Chiefs stadium will remain outside of the city and be surrounded by parking lots.

These parking lots will be "built specifically to enhance the tailgating experience".

Manica is designing the stadium with HNTB as architect of record. The studios, which are both based in Kansas City, were selected ahead of a proposal from another Kansas City firm, Populous.

Read:

What will the future stadium look like?

"We are incredibly fortunate that Kansas City is home to world-class sports and entertainment design talent, and that has been on full display throughout this process," said Kansas City Chiefs president Mark Donovan.

"David Manica and the Manica team stood out throughout a rigorous months-long process, honoring and embracing our history while presenting a bold and dynamic vision for the future. "

"It is the honor of a lifetime to be entrusted with designing the next home of the Kansas City Chiefs in our hometown," added Manica founder David Manica.

"My entire team is committed to creating a stadium that honors the legacy, tradition, and unmatched energy of Arrowhead while boldly reimagining its future," he continued.

"This stadium is being designed not just for today's fans, but for the generations of Chiefs Kingdom to come – a place that reflects the passion, pride, and enduring strength of one of the greatest fan bases in all of sports."

Recently, numerous NFL teams have unveiled new stadiums, including the Washington Commanders, while the Buffalo Bills stadium is set to open later this year.

The images are by Manica.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a proposal for a waterside repair and reuse hub exploring craft, material reuse and environmental stewardship is among projects from the University of Plymouth.

Also featured is a regenerative laboratory restoring Plymouth Sound's seabed and a proposal to transform polluted harbour water into a resource for marine research, industry and public engagement.

University of Plymouth

Institution: University of Plymouth
School: School of Art, Design and Architecture
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture and Master of Architecture
Tutors: Alessandro Aurigi, Nikolina Bobic, Ricky Burke, Graham Devine, Mathew Emmett, Andy Humphreys and Sana Murrani

School statement:

"Architecture at the University of Plymouth is explored as a civic, environmental and material practice. The work asks how buildings, landscapes and institutions can support social and ecological life, and how design can shape futures responsive to the conditions of the present.

"Across undergraduate and postgraduate projects, students examine architecture as a way of connecting people, resources, knowledge and place.

"The projects showcased here focus on two settings of civic and environmental consequence in Plymouth: the working waterfront and the university campus.

"Postgraduate students worked through live engagement with Plymouth Fisheries and related stakeholders to reimagine the Fish Quay after the closure of the fish auction, asking how waterfront renewal might support the coexistence of small-scale fisheries, public access, marine ecology, local food economies and climate adaptation.

"Undergraduate students examined the university as a contested civic and knowledge institution through projects centred on the Students' Union, Campus Park and wider city connections.

"Throughout, architecture is framed as relationships between labour and ecology, institution and public life, material systems and long-term stewardship.

"Proposals for adaptive reuse, flexible adaptation and low-carbon material systems rethink how buildings are occupied, maintained and shared, supporting practices that can change over time."

Aperture Obscura: Mechanisms of Perception by Libby Volokh

"Aperture Obscura positions itself within Plymouth's reconstructed civic landscape as a mediator between everyday urban life and the distant realities of contemporary conflict and displacement.

"Located on Armada Way, a post-war axis shaped by wartime destruction and institutional reconstruction, the project explores how architecture can hold unresolved histories and present anxieties simultaneously.

"Through film, archive, and collective occupation, it seeks to recover voices obscured by conflict, drawing on the work of Martha Rosler, Paul Virilio and Gilles Deleuze.

"The adaptive reuse of the abandoned Salvation Army Congress Hall resists demolition, material extraction, replacement and civic erasure through reconstruction."

Student: Libby Volokh
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Mathew Emmett and Nikolina Bobic
Email: elizabethvolokh[at]gmail.com

Civic Assemblage by Ciaran Halpin

"What is the future role of the university? As institutions increasingly advocate lifelong learning, existing pedagogical frameworks struggle to support evolving relationships between education, industry and public life.

"Conventional models of teaching risk becoming isolated from the realities of material production and civic engagement.

"The Civic Assemblage emerges as an investigation into this condition, reimagining the university as an open, collaborative framework where making, learning and industry converge, thereby activating public participation and positioning education as a catalyst for social and urban transformation across Plymouth."

Student: Ciaran Halpin
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Ricky Burke and Alessandro Aurigi
Email: ciaran.halpin[at]outlook.com

Second Nature: Learning through Waste, Repair and Reuse by Holly Salmons

"This project addresses the UK's lack of education, responsibility and accountability around waste and recycling at both a national and domestic scale.

"Situated on the university's existing recycling centre, the project will localise the education and practice of upcycling and reuse.

"By involving students and the residents of Plymouth in practical lessons, and by making the sustainable, circular material processes that take place on site visible and integrated into public space, the project aims to change behaviours and attitudes towards over-consumption and carelessness regarding waste and recycling."

Student: Holly Salmons
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Andy Humphreys and Graham Devine
Email: hollsjs8[at]gmail.com

Pathologies of Place: Echoes of the Flesh by Freya Marchant

"Pathologies of Place retells narratives of bodies denied autonomy within Plymouth on both literal and socio-political levels.

"Examining the trajectory of the body, the project explores how certain bodies are pathologised and regulated through systems of care, control and spatial organisation, critiquing the influence of the Abercrombie Plan and scientific advancement in shaping perceptions of the body and space.

"The body is our basic means of having a world (Merleau-Ponty, 1945), yet it functions as a site of boundary-making (Butler, 1993), shaped by socio-political systems that tether it to normative and linear forms of being (Grosz, 1994).

"When disciplined and mechanised, the body is constrained by structures that enforce a predetermined trajectory (Betson, 2015).

"Can embodiment escape linearity in systems designed around a single privileged body? The project redistributes the body onto the building itself, producing moments of heightened proprioception.

"The building becomes responsive and metamorphic, adapting to Plymouth's landscape through Arduino-based reactive systems.

"The project forms an archive in which, by encountering forgotten narratives of Plymouth, the inhabitant is prompted to relearn what it means to inhabit a body within a post-human condition."

Student: Freya Marchant
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Nikolina Bobic and Mathew Emmett
Email: freyapebbles[at]outlook.com

The Generative Library by Oliver Mowbray

"The traditional library of social exchange has become a temple to the Cartesian human. This adaptation to the university library ruptures physical, socio-economic and socio-cultural barriers, exposing students to exchange and collaboration whilst preserving physical media.

"Reclaimed rubble in gabion baskets holds a historic resonance that patinas with ecologies, appropriation and adaptation.

"Architecture here is generated through occupation and living memory; non-human elements act as responsive participants, a pulsating reactor, expanding and contracting.

"Extended landings and crossings, whilst unmoving, allow a 'movement that is both integrative and exploratory' (Leatherbarrow, 2009, p. 224), inspiring serendipitous encounters and informal collaborative learning."

Student: Oliver Mowbray
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Ricky Burke and Alessandro Aurigi
Email: ojmowbray[at]outlook.com

Data for Democracy by Yola Troughton

"Data for Democracy aims to reclaim the power of digital data held by the opaque hands of a few, redistributing it democratically back into our own regional systems.

"By empowering and protecting our local civic infrastructure as we move into the new digital age, the scheme looks to a more socially and environmentally sustainable approach to data storage and handling, integrating citizens' assemblies and other civic workshops alongside a digital archive.

"Acting as an engine, the data centre powers discourse through access to contextualised information, while the excess thermal energy is harnessed through passive heating strategies to support the functions of the building."

Student: Yola Troughton
Course: ARCH6002 Design Studio and Professional Practice, BA (Hons) Architecture
Tutors: Andy Humphreys and Graham Devine
Email: yola.troughton[at]gmail.com

Molecular Microplasti[cities]: Degradation as Disclosure by Charlie Hirst

"Molecular Microplasti[cities] addresses the growing threat of microplastic pollution in marine ecosystems.

"Located at Sutton Harbour, the project retrofits existing infrastructure to transform polluted harbour water into a resource for research, industry and public engagement.

"Water is purified through two filtration towers integrated into the architecture and then reused to support aquaculture, marine research and fish market operations.

"The towers also house modular living pods for researchers and fishing industry workers. By making the invisible visible — revealing the hidden presence of microplastics through architecture — the project becomes a monument to environmental change, promoting awareness, collaboration and sustainable marine regeneration."

Student: Charlie Hirst
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Mathew Emmett and Sana Murrani
Email: charlie_daniel[at]hotmail.co.uk

The Seabed Laboratory by Ben Howley

"The Seabed Laboratory responds to the long-term ecological decline of Plymouth Sound, where centuries of dredging and trawling have left soft scars across the seabed.

"The project treats these scars as opportunities for repair, positioning Fish Quay as a place where fishing communities and marine ecologists work together to restore the Sound.

"The old auction building is grafted onto new structures that support hatcheries, laboratories and seagrass workshops, while a recycled steel warehouse produces shellcrete reefs from waste scallop shells.

"A shellcrete tower shaped by kelp holdfasts marks the quay as a renewed landmark of restoration."

Student: Ben Howley
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Sana Murrani and Mathew Emmett
Email: benhowley3[at]gmail.com

[RE]Imagining Resilience Through System Thinking by Alastair Freeman

"Regenerative design extends beyond traditional sustainability by actively repairing ecosystems and enhancing the capacity of future generations to thrive.

"This proposal seeks to recycle waste from the fishing industry into seagrass pods that restore rare marine habitats in Plymouth Sound, an area where climate change poses significant threats to biodiversity.

"Repurposing this waste establishes a circular model that regenerates the marine food web while delivering enduring ecological and human benefits.

"Ultimately, the project aims to transform the built environment into resilient, productive habitats that support both natural ecosystems and human communities."

Student: Alastair Freeman
Course: ARCH766 Design Praxis, Master of Architecture
Tutors: Sana Murrani and Mathew Emmett
Email: freeman.alastair[at]gmail.com

In Mutual Dependence – Mending through material, craft and environment by Zi Jie Chan

"The project proposes a pavilion that rethinks construction through mutual dependence, where material, environment and users are interlinked rather than controlled.

"In Plymouth's maritime context of shipbuilding and repair, as well as Devon's regenerative woodland practices, it uses timber offcuts, reclaimed sail and rope to form a low-tech, reversible structure.

"Instead of resisting coastal forces such as salt, humidity and wind, the design embraces processes of weathering, mending and adaptation, allowing it to evolve over time.

"This project challenges conventional construction methods based on permanence and extraction, instead promoting circular, craft-based architecture grounded in material awareness, reuse and ongoing care."

item.content:encoded:
Continuing our Future Stadium series, we look at the revamp of the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu in Madrid, Spain, which shows how an existing stadium can be future-proofed.

Although numerous stadiums are built from the ground up every year, the reality is that many of the world's future stadiums already exist. Modern stadiums are some of the world's largest and most carbon-intensive buildings, and renovating them to extend their life is becoming increasingly important.

The extensive renovation of the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, by GMP Architekten with L35 and Ribas & Ribas, demonstrates how an almost 80-year-old structure can be transformed to meet the 24/7 commercial needs of the world's biggest football club – Real Madrid.

"I think the big driver for the stadium's development is basically the full-time use," GMP Architekten director Martin Glass told Dezeen.

"You build an installation that is incredibly expensive, so you don't want to only use it for two hours a week, and in that context, of course, the question of flexibility becomes a major driver," he continued.

"So, the more things you can do – more bigger events, smaller events, events in parallel – and the more you can integrate a stadium within the community, the more you can make it something more than just a sports venue."

Originally opened in 1947, the stadium has since seen several ad-hoc renovations and expansions.

Costing over €1 bn, which Glass pointed out is "a lot of money for renovation", the latest revamp gave the stadium a complete overhaul, while maintaining the "identity, soul and character of the existing structure".

Along with elevating the experience of fans on match days, the renovation had two major goals – to enhance the brand of Real Madrid and improve the commercial potential of the building.

Visually, the most obvious aspect of the renovation is its new facade. GMP Architekten wrapped the original concrete structure entirely in stainless steel louvres to give the building, and the club, a new identity.

"The most striking feature of the renovation is, of course, the new facade and roof – these shiny bands of stainless steel that we wrapped around the stadium," said Glass.

"The original stadium had a concrete structure that was actually quite visible, but it was also a bit outdated and came from a time when stadiums were [thought] more as engineering tasks," he continued.

"We're living in this internet and Instagram world where the image becomes more and more important. Real Madrid are aware of this and wanted to create a visually striking image."

Although the stadium was entirely wrapped in this shiny facade, the overhaul of the money-generating capacity of the stadium represented a huge portion of the design effort.

This expansion was achieved through numerous additions that allow the building to be more widely used on non-match days. A retractable roof was added, a retractable pitch built, a new museum created, markets and food stands enhanced and a new panoramic viewpoint is planned for the heights of the structure.

Perhaps the most impressive of these additions is the Bernabéu's retractable pitch. Key components of a modern stadium, retractable pitches allow for the main arena to be regularly utilised without damaging the playing surface.

Most commonly, this involves creating a playing surface that can be lifted and rolled off the pitch – such as at Tottenham Stadium in London.

Read:

Ten stadiums of the future that rewrite the playbook

However, as the Estadio Santiago Bernabéu is surrounded by roads on all sides, this was not possible and instead the pitch is stacked in a giant, underground greenhouse.

"It's a very brave client that trusts technology, but it also comes from a necessity," said Glass. "Because of this super tight inner city situation, a solution like Tottenham, or Schalke here in Germany, where the retracted pitch just goes outside, which is of course way easier to build, is simply not possible."

"They have residential areas all around them and public streets, so there simply wasn't any possibility to do something other than stack it underground," he continued. "Also, the reason that they stack it on just one side is that on the other side, 50 metres underneath the pitch, they have a public metro line."

Along with the retractable pitch, the retractable roof allows the main arena to be quickly converted for use for concerts and other large-scale events.

Beyond the main arena, the architecture studios developed attractions for fans on non-match days that would go beyond the standard stadium tours, including a new museum, which was built on a bridge between two of the existing, concrete stair towers.

"The museum is actually a 150-metre-long bridge that is cantilevering above the ground because they were not allowed to build on public ground," said Glass.

"Only the Museo del Prado has more visitors [in Spain] than the Real Madrid Museum, and they are really expanding it a lot. The last time I was there, the prices were around 35 euros a visit, so it is absolutely a revenue generator."

The stadium also incorporates several restaurants, a brewery, Starbucks and the Bernabéu Market, which Real Madrid describes as a gastronomic district, all of which are open daily.

Following its renovation, the Santiago Bernabéu is set to host games at the upcoming World Cup in 2030, which takes place in Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. We recently rounded up all 23 stadiums that will host games at the tournament.

The photography is by Marcus Bredt.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture studio HYAN has renovated Green Sandwich House, a 1970s home in Japan, using a palette of timber, plaster and tiles to bring "warmth and texture" to a flexible, open living space.

Named after its setting enveloped by wooded hills in Hayama, south of Tokyo, Green Sandwich House was renovated for HYAN's founders, architect Anna Naganuma and designer Shohei Hasegawa.

Originally constructed in the late 1970s, the home required significant structural reinforcement to meet modern seismic codes, which the studio took as an opportunity to create airy, flexible interiors around the grid of the retained structural frame.

"The starting point was to inherit the house rather than demolish it. Preserving a 1970s house wasn't the goal in itself; we wanted to read the potential of the existing frame and update it for how we live today," Hasegawa told Dezeen.

"As both the designers and the residents, we don't see this as a finished work, but as a house that grows with our daily life," he added.

On the ground floor, almost all of the home's interior partitions were removed to create a single living, dining and kitchen space, with zoning created by changes in floor level and ceiling height.

The living area occupies a double-height space next to the kitchen and dining area, while alongside, the floor steps down slightly to create a lounge area with a nook for a daybed that can be closed off with patterned curtains.

This open layout, along with a simple material palette of pale plastered walls and timber floors, emphasises the presence of the reinforced timber columns and roof beams of the existing structure, which also suggest where the former partition walls once stood.

"Rather than dividing the kitchen, pantry, study and doma with walls, we connected them loosely as a single continuous space," explained Hasegawa.

"Work, daily life, hobbies and hosting friends all overlap naturally, while light, air and the surrounding scenery move through the whole house and give it a different character depending on the time of day and season," he added.

Read:

Kenta Hirayama clads House in Kinuta in steel-sheet facade

The interior surfaces are complemented by coloured tiles and terrazzo in the kitchen and bathroom, chosen in response to the play of light and shadow through the large windows and surrounding trees.

A staircase to one side of the ground floor space leads up to the more private first floor, which contains the home's bedrooms and a study overlooking the double-height living area.

"Wood, plaster and textiles - things with warmth and texture - kept alongside a restrained palette, so that the existing frame remains the protagonist," Hasegawa told Dezeen.

"More than being beautiful on their own, the materials matter for how they catch natural light and shadow and the changing seasons, tying the architecture, the landscape and daily life together," he added.

Elsewhere in Japan, the creation of a single, continuous living space was also central to House in Takahatayama by HYG Architects, and Kenta Hirayama clad a contemporary Tokyo home in steel sheets.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlassian Central skyscraper, designed by SHoP Architects and BVN Architecture, in Sydney, Australia, has become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

Designed as the Sydney headquarters for technology company Atlassian, the 180-metre-high office tower topped out earlier this week.

With a hybrid structure of timber, steel and concrete it overtakes the 86.6 -metre-high Ascent tower in Milwaukee, USA, by almost 100 metres, to become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

The 39-storey skyscraper has a unique hybrid structural system, with concrete cores supporting mass timber floors and internal structures, wrapped in a steel exoskeleton.

This exoskeleton supports seven "mega floors" that have been placed every four stories to divide the building vertically into what the design team described as "habitats".

These, primarily timber, habitats will contain office accommodation along with multi-floor atriums and elevated parks.

"SHoP has been privileged with the opportunity to design such an innovative project – one that we believe will redefine how people come together, collaborate, and create in Sydney and beyond," said SHoP Architects associate principal Andreia Teixeira.

"It's particularly rewarding to begin experiencing the spatial qualities of a high-rise that reimagines a natural habitat within an urban tower – connecting people to each other, nature and to the city around them," she continued.

"We're excited by how this concept sets a new benchmark for sustainability, where timber, landscape, and natural ventilation come together to shape a more holistic work-life experience and inspire future innovation."

According to the design team, the use of timber has reduced the overall building weight and carbon impact, while the steel and concrete ensures strength and stability.

The design expects the design to reduce the upfront embodied carbon by 50 per cent compared to a conventional steel and concrete office tower.

The team aims to also achieve a 50 per cent improvement in operational energy efficiency compared to a conventional 5 Star NABERS base building.

Read:

Studio Gang exposes mass-timber structure of Rubenstein Treehouse at Harvard

"Hybrid mass timber has done more than reduce embodied carbon, it has fundamentally shaped how tower buildings can be delivered, enabling prefabrication, dry construction and a faster, lighter vertical build," said BVN principal Peter Titmuss.

"As a prototype for mass-timber towers of the future, this is a moment of global significance."

The tower sits next to Sydney Central Station and was built over an existing historic building called The Parcels Shed that was once used for taking deliveries of parcels and then turned into a youth hostel.

SHoP Architects and BVN plan to incorporate the youth hostel building into the lower levels of the tower.

The project is set to complete by the end of this year with facade installation currently being completed.

New York-based SHoP Architects was founded in 1996.

The practice has completed a series of monumental tower designs including 111 W 57th Street on Billionaires Row in Manhattan and Brooklyn's first supertall skyscraper.

BVN is an Australian architecture firm that has offices in Sydney, Brisbane, London and New York.

It recently joined forces with Copenhagen studio 3XN on projects such as Sydney Fish Market and Quay Quarter Tower in Sydney, which was named Best Tall Building Worldwide by the Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat in 2023.

The photography is by Toby Peet.

item.content:encoded:
The Glasgow School of Art has announced that it cannot afford to rebuild the iconic Mackintosh Building without external funding, following the second fire that tore through the building in 2018.

According to an announcement made by the school yesterday, it has insufficient funds to reinstate the 1910 building by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, and it now plans to remove scaffolding surrounding the building to stabilise and expose its burned-out shell.

However, it said it will look to secure external funding to help enable reinstating the Mackintosh Building in the future.

"The school cannot possibly, on its own, rebuild this whole building," according to its chair of the board of governors Ann Priest.

"It would take us away from financial sustainability," she told the BBC.

Restoration "beyond the capacity and expertise of the school"

The announcement follows the settlement of a long-running arbitration claim with the building insurers regarding the 2018 blaze. Details of what was awarded have not been disclosed, but the school said it had offered "financial clarity" about what was possible.

It now estimates the cost of a full reinstatement to be around £265 million, which is "equivalent to five times the GSA's annual turnover" and four times more than a previous £62 million estimate.

"The scale of such a project would be beyond the capacity and expertise of the school and, despite reaching a positive settlement with insurers, the funding gap is significant due in large part to the rising costs of construction projects," said the report.

Priest added the Glasgow School of Art (GSA) is now looking for "visionary individuals" who could bring "serious investment" to the project, reported the BBC.

Scaffolding to be removed to expose shell

Affectionately known as the Mack, the fire-torn art school was the best-known building designed by Mackintosh, Scotland's most famous architect.

The first fire ripped through the art school in 2014, before a second, more destructive fire occurred in 2018 during a £35 million restoration project.

With restoration works now on hold, the school plans to remove the scaffolding that wraps the building and stabilise its shell with a mix of temporary and permanent internal supports.

The report outlines several options for moving forward, including partial reinstatement of the building. It also suggests the potential for the anchor of a "creative and cultural production innovation district", including nearby cultural institutions.

GSA's announcement has come as bad news to many who recognise the building as an iconic landmark in Scotland. Among them is architect Alan Dunlop, who described the announcement as "opaque".

Announcement is "travesty of epic proportions"

"What disappoints me most is the statement from the chair of governors saying that the Mackintosh can "have a new purpose and become a catalyst for innovation, regeneration and economic growth for Glasgow'," he wrote on Instagram.

"This seems to me to be a dilution of responsibility, and worse, a distinct failure to focus on their prime task of delivering a replacement for the Mackintosh building, rather than some centre for creative activity. It's clear to me still that a trust has to be set up, separate from the board."

In another post, he added "it is now clear that Mackintosh’s masterwork is gone forever", and called for efforts to retain as much as what is left as possible.

"For that we need an exceptional architect and a proper procurement process, not one like before that emphasises fee over talent and which recognises that this is the most important commission in Scotland and probably the UK," he wrote.

Meanwhile, Historic England's heritage at risk projects officer Lisa Rigg said it was an "absolute travesty of epic proportions".

"Where is the 21st-century Carnegie? Or the high-net-worth individuals, some of whom own swathes of the Scottish Highlands, ready to step in and save this iconic and pioneering art school building in its hour of need?" she wrote on LinkedIn.

Read:

Investigation into Glasgow School of Art fire fails to find "definitive cause"

In a shared statement, the Royal Institute of British Architects and Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland called on the government to help with the rebuild.

"We need leadership from the Scottish and UK Governments to find the resources needed to ensure the faithful reinstatement of the Mackintosh Building, and to secure its future as a revitalised creative hub serving Glasgow, Scotland and the world," read the statement.

In 2022, an inquiry into the cause of the second fire at the building failed to conclude due to insufficient evidence.

However, the report revealed that fifty per cent of the building was alight within 38 minutes of the firefighters arriving at the site. It is believed that this "uncontrolled fire growth and rapid development" was exacerbated by the restoration works.

Shortly after the second blaze, the former director of the Glasgow School of Art Tom Inns said that it would be rebuilt.

"It is as vital a part of the Glasgow School of Art's future as it has been for the last 100 years," Inns told Dezeen at the time. "We will rebuild so that 'the Mack' can continue to provide creative inspiration to students, staff and visitors."
