item.content:encoded:
Our cities are full of apartment blocks dotted with pathetically sized balconies too small to be of any actual use, writes Jessica Furseth.

If no one ever sits there, is a balcony still a balcony? I found myself pondering this question as I was walking the perimeter of the Isle of Dogs in East London, an area where new blocks of flats seem to pop up like mushrooms.

These river-facing balconies should have made a great place to sit on that lovely summer evening, but save for the occasional lone smoker, they appeared deserted. There's a simple explanation, of course: the balconies are just too small.

Developers know they can charge more for this ephemeral idea with only a tokenistic gesture towards it

You know the ones – they are absolutely everywhere in most major cities around the world. They're cut into the face of a housing block, or sometimes hanging off the wall, measuring little more than a metre deep and two across, often facing a loud and dusty road.

That's just enough space for you, during the initial property viewing, to step outside and exclaim, "Oh there's a balcony!" This is the best moment you'll ever have out on that thing, because it's too poky to be of any real use.

They fit a drying rack, maybe a bicycle (my ex had a bike stolen off his balcony three floors up, which was frankly impressive). You can just about squeeze in that dinky table and chair set from IKEA, the Tärnö that's advertised as "a perfect size for the balcony".

Read:

Ten buildings that make a sculptural feature of their balconies

But this isn't Paris, where people survey the cityscape below over croissants and coffee – this is Hackney, where balconies with dirty railings are choking in the road dust from Mare Street, empty in the gorgeous sunset.

And yet, we continue to build them. The pandemic really impressed upon us the benefit of private outdoor space, as a place to enjoy fresh air without risk. It's not about the virus anymore, but perhaps some fear of the commons lingers.

Size notwithstanding, balconies do carry a lot of outdoor feelings – there's a sense of breathing space, and outdoor seclusion is a little exciting. Developers and estate agents know they can charge more for this ephemeral idea with only a tokenistic gesture towards it, whose practical uselessness is only revealed once we've moved in. By then, the money has already changed hands.

Even Juliet on her namesake balcony was close enough to speak to Romeo

Long before the pandemic pressed the issue of separate balconies, the idea was a feature in evolved societies: people should have decent housing, and if they can't have a garden they should at least have a veranda.

But while a concrete box on the 20th floor will provide air, it gives people none of the social functions of the garden. Even Juliet on her namesake balcony was close enough to speak to Romeo.

"At 100 feet, the balcony loses all social connection with the ground," writes Alistair Cartwright, an architectural historian at the University of Liverpool. "One cannot imagine calling up for a lapel pin and a loaf of bread to one of these postwar balconies, as the destitute poet Albert Llanas is said to have done to an old acquaintance in 1920s Barcelona."

Read:

Bright yellow balconies enliven Melbourne apartment block by Austin Maynard Architects

Today, urban conversations about terraces are primarily about light and air, not connection to our neighbours and communities. National standards leave the details to local policies, but according to the London Housing Design Guide from the mayor of London, "private outside space is desirable in all circumstances". The total size depends on the number of occupants, but a balcony should always be at least 1.5 metres deep.

The guide does say that this space can be added to the inside of the house in exceptional circumstances. I would have loved that when I lived in Haggerston, east London, where I had a balcony I'm pretty sure was slimmer than regulation.

It faced a narrow courtyard like in the Alfred Hitchcock film Rear Window, and the sensation of surveillance was a strong deterrent from enjoyment. Adding insult to injury, that terrace also cut into my miniscule living room, and I would have far preferred to have that space inside instead.

Another option is to trade private outdoor space for more public amenities

In New York, the balconies are even tinier than in London – a report by Curbed found several examples at just 45 centimetres width, and not even IKEA can help you with that. Architect and zoning expert Walter Marin grew philosophical when asked by Curbed to comment on this level of stinginess, speculating that New York balconies may not actually be about spending time out there, but more like a cold plunge. The point is to step outside for a moment and take a deep breath, before heading back inside.

Even as people admit to getting little use out of their diminutive balconies, I've found my suggestion to get rid of them altogether a hard sell. ("It's not great, but it's fine," my boyfriend Tom said about his ridiculous terrace, a trifle defensively.)

But there are alternatives. On a recent train journey out of Waterloo station I noticed how balconies facing the rail tracks were enclosed to protect them from noise and dust. Part of the new developments in Nine Elms, south London, these glazed, ventilated winter gardens are a way to enjoy such space year-round, wasting nothing.

Read:

"An architectural style has emerged that I'm calling 'gentleism'"

Other countries are also building these enclosed terraces. A walk past new waterfront developments in Tallinn, Estonia, for example, will showcase dozens of buildings with balconies featuring a glass pane that can be opened or closed depending on the weather. A tiny balcony thus becomes a light-filled bonus room in winter, when the temperature can stay below freezing for months at a time.

Another option is to trade private outdoor space for more public amenities. Maybe you don't get your own balcony, but there's a roof garden, or a new park nearby. In south London, Lambeth Council requires new developments to have at least 50 square metres of shared amenity space, in addition to 10 square metres of private balcony space per flat.

Many London councils have similar rules to Lambeth where, if amenity space can't be provided on-site, the money can go to an off-site provision. The challenge, as ever, is ensuring that what gets delivered is of sufficient quality – there are also far too many bleak, concreted plazas permanently in the shade.

It might be better to put that square footage back inside homes where it can be of use

I gave up on tiny balconies for good after my Hitchcock situation in Haggerston. These days I prefer going to the park – even though I share it with innumerable dogs and runners (both off-leash and equally prone to bumping into you), I far prefer the greenery and feeling of open space.

Private terraces for all is a nice idea, but it doesn't seem to be working for people; we're just not using our tiny balconies. Yes, we need outdoor space, but they aren't meeting our needs.

It might be better to put that square footage back inside homes where it can be of use, and turn our focus towards making better communal outdoor space. If given a choice between a useless balcony where I'm alone with my drying rack, or a green garden shared with my neighbours, I know what I'd choose.

Jessica Furseth is a journalist based in London. Her writing has appeared in The Guardian, Vox, Time Out, Huck, The Cut, Atlas Obscura, Vice, The Independent, and elsewhere.

item.content:encoded:
Design studios Softlab and Moment Factory have created seven immersive installations for the 350-metre-high Edge NYC skyscraper viewpoint at Hudson Yards, including a massive kaleidoscope and a series of pulsating globes.

Edge NYC, which is the highest indoor-outdoor sky deck in the Western Hemisphere, is set on the 100th floor of Kohn Pedersen Fox's 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper.

The recently opened, immersive installations are intended to create an additional experience to its bird's-eye view of Manhattan. Similar to ones designed by art collective TeamLab, the artworks were created to be walked through and experienced in person.

Among the first installations in the visitor route is Pulse, which was designed by Softlab and features 450 pulsating globes across a number of rooms that shift in colour as visitors walk past them.

"Pulse is really about capturing the energy of New York City," Softlab director Michael Szivos told Dezeen.

"The 450 globes represent the city as a world within worlds, while the shifting gradients and interactive choreography reflect how individual actions contribute to the collective energy of the city."

The studio hoped that the installation would evoke "a sense of curiosity" and aimed for it to change with each visit.

"The colour palette is derived from Edge's brand colours, which are inspired by the changing colours of the sky throughout the day – from midday to sunset and twilight," Szivos said.

"We organised these into warm and cool gradients that continuously shift and transition, allowing the installation to move between contrasting atmospheres through generative behaviours, so the experience is never exactly the same twice."

Also among the installations is Kaleidoscope, a series of rooms that includes a main artwork that Edge NYC says is "New York's largest kaleidoscope" and was designed by Moment Factory.

"The goal was to design an interior experience that acts as a mirror to the city's dynamic nature," Moment Factory creative director Patrick Bisson told Dezeen.

"By treating the space as a prism that refracts New York's radiant energy, we provide a distinct sensory engagement that complements the outdoor sky deck before visitors even step outside."

The largest kaleidoscope lets visitors step inside it to be surrounded by shifting, colourful prisms in changing patterns.

"The installation was designed to function as a multifaceted prismatic space, integrating digital media with highly reflective architectural surfaces," Bisson said.

"This approach captures the physical movement of the visitors, blending their reflections directly into the content," he continued.

"The result is a complex matrix of shifting geometry and light, creating a multiplicity of reflections that ensures an infinite, constantly evolving spatial experience."

Read:

New York's art deco icons inform revamped restaurant at The Edge

As well as the main kaleidoscope, Moment Factory also created numerous smaller kaleidoscopes, including one featuring street photography of New York City.

"The smaller kaleidoscope is designed as an intimate moment for guests to connect directly with the fabric of the city," Bisson said.

"We curated a street photography aesthetic that highlights urban textures and architectural geometry, interspersed with iconic landmarks."

The immersive installations also include Reflections, a kinetic sculpture made from 200 mirrored surfaces, and Crystal Cave, a 25-foot canopy of giant crystals, among others.

While most of the installations are located on the same floor as the Edge NYC viewpoint itself, there is also Skyrise, a "cinematic elevator experience" and Prism, an entryway experience that shows shifting views of New York.

The overall designs were all inspired by Edge itself, according to experience agency Journey, which oversaw the strategy for the project.

"We examined what already made Edge NYC so distinctive: its angular and triangular architecture, its use of glass and light, and its powerful vantage point to offer visitors new perspectives of New York City – both physically and mentally," said Journey strategy and creative lead Olivia Reid.

"From this foundation – and the visual language of triangles and prismatic energy – the strategic process enabled us to set and safeguard the experiential vision."

The Edge also features the newly revamped restaurant Peak designed by Journey, while other Hudson Yards attractions include Heatherwick Studio's Vessel and The Shed venue, which features a telescoping roof.

item.content:encoded:
Designer Audrey Levy has reimagined a common household appliance with her project How to Grow a Refrigerator, applying sustainable insulating and cooling technologies that take advantage of the power of bacteria and the sun.

The refrigerator, alternatively titled Xero Cool, is a compact, soft capsule made out of bacterial cellulose xerogel – a light, highly insulating and naturally compostable alternative to the expanded plastic foams inside conventional fridges.

The Central Saint Martins (CSM) graduate imagines it being paired with an electricity-free cooling system based on solar thermal energy, where heat from the sun is captured via a rooftop solar collector and used to drive a cooling cycle.

This would drastically lower the greenhouse gas emissions that currently come from refrigeration's large electricity demands and the leaking of cooling gases, Levy argued, while also challenging our relationship with technology and food.

"Researching refrigeration became a surprisingly radicalising experience," Levy told Dezeen. "It felt like uncovering this seedy underbelly of civilisation connected to so many critical functions of modern society."

"The domestic refrigerator is just the tip of a global network of continuous cold space that spans the globe, connecting production and consumption," she continued. "Our overwhelming reliance on this technology presents a conceptually rich but terrifying paradox: as climate extremes intensify, so does our reliance on refrigeration."

"At the same time, refrigeration technology is responsible for eight per cent of global emissions, roughly three times that of the entire aviation industry. So the way we manufacture cold actually makes the Earth hotter."

As she researched, Levy came to believe that transforming the technology behind refrigeration would also involve updating its "heavy, clunky" and "sterile" aesthetic, which she found has remained largely unchanged since the early 20th century, when the appliance was launched and marketed as a symbol of status and food safety to anxious mothers.

"The legacy of plastic whiteness as cleanliness lives on in many of today's interiors," the designer explained.

The look of Levy's fridge instead communicates the nature of its material construction, which combines bacterial cellulose xerogel with further insulating felted wool.

Read:

Open-source Re:Mix blender works with household jars

It combines the softness of a domestic object with a hint of "solarpunk" – the social and artistic movement that imagines positive futures built on sustainable technologies.

Bacterial cellulose xerogel is, like other types of bacterial cellulose, a bacteria-grown biomaterial. But it has a rigid, low-density structure similar to the expanded plastic foams used for packaging and insulation.

Levy made hers to her own recipe in the CSM Grow Lab using only non-toxic materials, unlike the plastics and refrigerants in regular fridges.

Lining the inside of the fridge are macrofluidic panels that circulate cooled water to draw away heat while also protecting the absorbent wool and xerogel from direct contact with food.

Levy's vision for her fridge of the future is that the fuzzy, insulating layers will be effective enough so that the fridge does not require constant electrically generated cooling.

Instead, it will use a solar-thermal absorption refrigeration system, which is triggered by the heat of the sun during the day, setting off a chain of passive state changes in an absorbent material and liquid refrigerant.

Read:

Ganni unveils handbag made from bacterial leather at LDF

The next stage of the project will involve Levy realising this system by connecting the fridge to a dish-like outdoor solar collector as well as simple copper condenser and evaporator coils on top of the fridge.

Even though absorption refrigeration is typically seen as less efficient than the electrically powered compression systems in conventional fridges, it is Levy's preferred method, because she sees power grids as being at risk from increasing demand and the transition to renewable energy as potentially being incomplete for a long time.

Absorption refrigeration also avoids the need for solar panels or battery storage, with their requirement for large amounts of mined minerals. It has no moving parts, cutting down on complexity and maintenance, and operates almost silently.

Based on recent scientific research, the designer believes the system can be made entirely with bio-based ingredients, with activated carbon and ethanol as the absorbent and refrigerant, making the process more non-toxic and safe than ever before.

Levy's fridge is finished with a fruit bowl below the main unit, intended to invite external storage where appropriate. Currently, many items are commonly refrigerated though they do not require it, she says, while some – like tomatoes and bread – are actively damaged by the cooler temperatures.

"I would hope that the world in which this alternative refrigerator was adopted would be a reality in which we have re-evaluated relationships with the kitchen, food and material cultures," said Levy. "Perhaps spatial constraints would prompt more intentional consumption."

Read:

Solar Metal Smelter uses giant magnifying glass to melt metal

"A lower coefficient of performance and non-continuous cooling cycles would mean increased mindfulness of when the fridge is open and for how long," she added. "Transitioning to less efficient technologies that eliminate reliance on ecologically damaging processes and build local resilience is a challenge to revisit how we evaluate the merits of efficiency."

Levy created Xero Cool / How to Grow a Refrigerator as part of her graduate degree in Biodesign at CSM, from which she graduated in 2026. Other graduates in her cohort created projects including an audio player for listeners to co-compose music with artists and a low-tech communicator for Palestinian bus drivers.

item.content:encoded:
Flooring manufacturer Forbo has revealed how agricultural waste from cacao production has been repurposed into flooring that supports cacao-growing communities in West Africa in this exclusive video produced by Dezeen.

According to the brand, Marmoleum Cocoa is made from up to 98 per cent natural raw materials including linseed oil, wood flour and jute.

The flooring incorporates discarded cocoa shells sourced through Kumasi Commodity Innovations, a Netherlands-based sustainable agritech company that upcycles discarded cacao fruit and other agricultural side-streams into juices and ingredients.

The video explores how local architecture studio KOKO used Marmoleum throughout Rae State Secondary School, which it designed in Jüri, Estonia.

According to interior architect Raili Paling, the flooring, which was made from Marmoleum, became the "main character" of the school's interiors due to both its sustainable credentials and visual qualities.

"We had a vision to use very sustainable products," Paling said. "[Marmoleum] has this special light reflection; it's sophisticated and contemporary."

Principal interior architect Liis Lindvere also highlighted the material's environmental benefits.

"It's a brilliant way to reuse waste from [cacao] production – not just as a filling material but as an aesthetic value as well," she said.

The natural variation in the cacao shells creates subtle differences in colour and tone, which Paling said contribute to a calming learning environment.

"In educational spaces, you need something that subconsciously calms you down," she said.

Outside of the aesthetic appeal, the architects were also drawn to the wider story behind the material and its potential to reduce the environmental impact of construction.

"Up to 40 per cent of the world's carbon emissions come from the built environment," Lindvere said. "So we have a huge responsibility to keep this planet safe."

The collaboration also provides an additional source of income for the West African farmers who supply the cacao.

Kumasi Commodity Innovations co-founder Linda Klunder explained how the process works.

"Kumasi started by increasing the income of West African farmers by upcycling the overlooked part of the cacao fruit," she said. "As part of our collaboration with Forbo, the wives of farmers from whom we source receive an additional income."

Read:

Forbo's Flotex flooring offers a "blank canvas" for designers

"We are showing that there is not just a one-dimensional application of the fruit," Klunder continued. "It's a story of circularity and also about human impact."

The photography is by Forbo and Tõnu Tunnel.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: architects' designs are being contained within digital files so big they can take two hours to load, leading to delays and mix-ups on projects, experts warned in a talk hosted by HP at the UIA World Congress of Architects 2026.

During the discussion, which took place in Barcelona, HP senior vice president and division president of advanced compute solutions Jim Nottingham warned that increasingly complex digital architectural models have become "massive".

"Data has been exploding or growing for several decades," Nottingham said. "Now with AI, it's growing exponentially faster."

"In reality, all the AEC – architecture, engineering and construction – customers that we work with, particularly architects, the model sizes are getting massive. And so I've been surprised to go on site and see teams loading their design, taking 90 minutes, two hours, just to load the design."

Nottingham added that managing this data and how it transitions between different tools is essential for removing friction from AEC workflows that can often lead to inefficiencies, errors or lost work.

"Waiting is the enemy... waiting reflects a point of friction, and those points of friction are usually where the opportunities come in for the design to drift," he said.

"Misinformation gives you the wrong trade-off, so when you look at everything that happens around the design and the workflow, all the transitions to different tools, all the handoffs, all the reviews, all of the work that happens outside. That's where you see people waiting."

Also on the panel, Nadeem Mir, head of technology and senior partner at global architecture studio Foster + Partners, explained that transitioning to 3D modelling in recent years has led to "an explosion of file sizes".

The huge and ever-expanding size of these files is a "runaway train" that is making collaboration with other studios and firms on projects "incredibly difficult", Mir added.

"I have people come to me saying, 'You've ruined my life because my client is complaining'. Because the interior designers that their client has chosen can't operate in our space, because they're a small interior designer and they're just not ready to do this level of computation," said Mir.

"We're definitely going to have to change and shift completely away from the current way of working, quite frankly," he added. "The kind of legacy of using file-based design is just not going to work anymore."

Joining Nottingham and Mir on the panel, HP senior vice president and division president for large-format print, Daniel Martinez, warned that such hugely complex architectural models are contributing to construction errors.

"The ability to represent a lot more information in that model, in the data, ultimately makes it much richer in the design phase, but it also makes it more complex in the build phase," he said.

"Today, it's estimated that close to 15 per cent of the cost of a construction project is related to reworks or mistakes that need to be redone, or inefficiencies in terms of the ability to represent the work in the real world," he added.

"And therefore, there's a real opportunity to streamline that process and make it much more efficient. I envision in the future that architects, as they present a project, will also be incorporated with a level of technology and a technology enablement that allows them to reduce that 15 per cent or 10 per cent of inefficiencies to 1 per cent or even below."

The talk, titled "Closing the distance between an idea and a building", focused on how technology can help ensure architectural intent is maintained through to the end of a project as construction becomes ever-more complex.

It included a discussion about AI, and how it might be able to assist architects.

Nottingham said that the initial design phase has already been "significantly accelerated for many architects" by image-generating AI diffusion models, but he predicted that the technology will also increasingly play a role in reducing tasks that architects tend to dislike.

"There's a tremendous opportunity that some people are starting to do, and I think you're going to start seeing a lot more people do," he said. "You can eliminate a lot of that friction with agentic AI that takes a lot of the mundane out and lets the creative brilliance stay in the flow, and the end-through, and it's going to be a big opportunity to eliminate a lot of the drift and a lot of the waiting."

"In this case, AI is not replacing the creative expertise; AI is eliminating all of the mundane work that gets in the way of creative expertise," he added.

Martinez revealed that HP is running pilots in some areas of an AI tool that would assess development plans and provide a chance of success for gaining approval based on local policies.

"Being able to accelerate that from what today takes 18, 24 months, and in some cases, to being able to do that within a few weeks, would be a phenomenal use of this technology that would also reduce the amount of effort on the administrative side," said Martinez.

"So I think there's ample opportunity to accelerate building, there's ample opportunity to reduce those efficiencies in ways that we talked about, and ultimately bring down the amount of work that architects need to spend on those mundane tasks that aren't adding value, or that aren't as enjoyable to them as we know, and as we hear, and ultimately free up more space for that creative work, and accelerating that creative work, and doing more of that," he added.

Mir said that Foster + Partners is looking to use AI tools trained on its own data sets.

While he agreed that AI has the potential to be "hugely helpful" for architects, he stressed the importance of understanding how the technology works and its limitations.

"I think there's a bit of fever going on at the moment, and we might need to calm down a little bit, but it also can be hugely helpful," he said. "I think the challenge here is making sure we understand where the opportunities are and target those opportunities; not doing AI for the sake of AI, doing it with a degree of caution and understanding."

"It's very, very difficult when – I mean – this literally is almost the definition of a black box, and you throw something at it, and it throws something back, and I think you need to have a level of understanding of what is going on in that black box, so that you can assess what's coming back in an objective way."

To find out more about HP, visit its website.

item.content:encoded:
For our Future Stadium series, we asked nine of the world's top stadium architects to predict the biggest shift in stadium design over the next 10 years.

To determine how stadium design will shift over the next decade, we asked each of the nine architects: "what will stadiums look like in the next 10 years and beyond?"

Rather than focusing on style or form, almost all the architects focused on what lies around a stadium – the red-hot trend of sports mixed-use districts, which we explored in depth earlier in the series.

The architects were also interested in what goes into a stadium, from healthier materials to the financing, showing that these days top firms are more than happy to play ball with the expanding needs of district developers and teams.

Read on for the thoughts of architects within some of the biggest stadium designers of our age.

Jim Heverin, board director, ZHA

"By 2036, we may see many new stadiums in English football, particularly Manchester, Newcastle, Chelsea and Birmingham. As someone who bid for the Birmingham City stadium, it's fair to say I didn't imagine it as a Victorian factory. Leaving that aside, I think the client's masterplan and brief in Birmingham is demonstrative of a trend that we can see shaping future stadiums.

"We have many new club owners, and many come to it with no background in football. What they bring is ambition and possibly an unsentimental business way of looking at the stadium.

"Birmingham City is looking to build what is already underway in Manchester City, an entertainment precinct. Not solely a new stadium but to surround it with other destinations and mix of uses such as an arena, a hotel, shopping. This should go some way to addressing the age-old issue with stadiums, which is their potential to be a sterile and empty place on non-match or event days.

"For their World Cup, the Saudis are proposing some interesting large-scale urban developments. The traditional stadium as a recognisable artifice is subsumed into a larger urban design where it's embedded, even hidden, within a larger cityscape. The Jeddah stadium is hidden within a city massing, think of Highbury, like so many older British stadiums with the stadium partially or fully surrounded by houses.

"Who would have thought that the historic British grounds are being reimagined in Jeddah?"

Martin Glass, director, GMP Architekten

"Stadiums are developing into more and more fully flexible, multi-purpose arenas, evolving from single-purpose sport facilities into broader mixed-use hybrids with the aim of 24/7 usage.

"We understand sustainability in future stadiums must extend far beyond installing solar panels or using recycled materials. 'Building less and adapting more', addresses one of the largest environmental impacts of a stadium: its construction.

"The biggest sustainability challenge may not be technological but urban. A stadium that is transit-connected, intensively used, integrated into the neighborhood, shared by multiple groups, beloved by society and adaptable over decades will be more sustainable than a technologically advanced stadium that sits largely empty.

"Venue design will not focus only on the traditional, typically male, core fan associated with the one typical core sports discipline. By broadening the type of events, but also with women's sports growing rapidly and attendance becoming more diverse, stadiums will need to reflect this much broader range of users.

"From the perspective of an architect, we see stadiums among the most compelling building types because they transcend the conventional role of architecture. They are not simply places that contain an activity; they amplify human emotion, memory, and collective identity."

John Rhodes, director of sports and entertainment, HOK 

"In many ways, the stadiums of 2035 are already being designed.

"The future of stadium design will be defined by a series of pragmatic but powerful shifts: from spectacle to experience, from singular purpose to continuous use, and from static architecture to adaptable systems.

"Historically, the defining metric has been the C-value – a measure of sightlines that ensures every seat can see the pitch. While this remains important, it is no longer sufficient. Advances in computational design allow us to move beyond a single parameter toward a more holistic 'entertainment value', combining comfort, proximity, acoustics, amenities and atmosphere into a layered experience.

"We are already seeing disruption in the traditional bowl configuration with dynamic movement in the upper tiers/back of the bowl, making them more vertical and responsive to variable events and fields of play. This shift toward individual experience sits alongside a broader transformation in how stadiums are used. Increasingly, they are no longer defined by sport alone.

"Climate change will also play a defining role. Rising temperatures and more extreme weather conditions are driving demand for adaptable environments, including retractable roofs and advanced cooling systems.

"Importantly, not all innovations will be digital. The enduring appeal of a live event lies in its shared, real-time experience. Technology will need to enhance, rather than compete with, that collective focus."

Bob van Bebber, director, Boogertman + Partners

"The future of stadium design in Africa is not about building the biggest, most advanced stadiums; it is about designing and developing the cities, communities and sports ecosystems around them.

"It's very easy to be seduced by visions of huge, billion-dollar stadiums, but the most important question is always: what happens after the tournament?

"To be sustainable, future African stadiums need to become community hubs that are used every day of the year, not just on big match days or for concerts. That means they should be co-located with other revenue-generating uses such as retail outlets or arenas.

"Civic services such as clinics, libraries, police, social grants services and transport nodes would also work well. The more you can bring together, the better. Without public transport, stadiums risk ending up like spaceships in a sea of parking.

"Winning hearts, however, is crucial. Parachuting in a foreign concept and decorating it with ill-considered African-inspired graphics won't do the trick. The role of the designer is to uncover the stories that matter to the communities the stadium will serve and express them through architecture.

"Moveable facilities could be used to test markets without committing to massive capital expenditure. Perhaps impermanent architecture should play a greater role in the development of sports infrastructure over the next decade."

Fred Ortiz, global practice director of sports and entertainment, HKS

"Over the next decade, stadiums will evolve from single-purpose venues into adaptable civic destinations that support sport, entertainment, tourism and everyday public life.

"The era of isolating stadiums on cheap land surrounded by parking is ending, replaced by integrated developments that anchor vibrant, year-round districts.

"Today's leading venues already serve as civic catalysts, combining flexible, enclosed designs with climate-responsive architecture that improves comfort through smarter approaches to heat, shade and ventilation while supporting a diverse calendar of events.

"The fan experience will become increasingly immersive, extending beyond the stadium into the surrounding precinct and to digital audiences worldwide. Ultimately, the most successful stadiums will be those that reflect the culture, history and identity of their communities—the venues their cities simply cannot imagine living without."

Colin Koop and Ryan Culligan, design partners, SOM

"The largest structures in our cities should be supercharged by our greatest ambitions. For too long, stadiums have been treated as short-lived containers for spectacle, surrounded by seas of asphalt, activated by episodic events, and often discarded long before the end of a reasonable lifespan.

"We have an opportunity to bring the park back to the ballpark. With a more rigorous, performance-driven approach to fabrication, material sourcing, and circularity, venues can move from carbon emitters to carbon sinks.

"Advances in low-carbon materials, clean energy, and digital fabrication have already opened the door.

"In designing the Queen's Braid, we have already explored how wood can meet the challenges of scale and long spans through an optimized woven timber shell. With their vast footprints and roof areas, stadiums can also become platforms for energy generation, and district-scale infrastructure.

"In the next decade, the best stadiums will be beautiful, civically engaged, and technically and environmentally ambitious."

Scott Capstack, head of design, Populous

"Over the next decade, the most successful stadiums will continue to be defined by how well architecture connects people, place and purpose, both inside and outside the venue.

"Stadiums will be valued by how connected they are to and within their surrounding community. These civic anchors will be part of a broader mixed-use district that allows for everyday activation beyond major events.

"The venue's architecture itself will become more flexible, enabling venues to evolve over time and accommodate changing sports and entertainment formats without requiring redevelopment. Projects like Highmark Stadium in Buffalo and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium with its retractable pitch demonstrate how future venues will seamlessly transition between events and experiences.

"From a technology perspective, it will become an invisible layer that enables more personalized experiences. Every facet of the fan experience will be connected digitally.

"The stadium of the future will be measured by more metrics than capacity and revenue. They must deliver measurable and lasting social, economic and civic value."

Frankie Sharpe, director of sports, BIG

"If the last 10 years tell us anything about the next 10, it's that technology will be the primary force reshaping the stadium experience, and the personal device has become central to all of it. A decade ago, mobile ticketing, real-time wayfinding, frictionless concessions, and augmented reality were all cutting-edge developments, but they have shifted to the baseline expectation at modern venues.

"As we look forward, the challenge for designers is to integrate new tools in ways that feel seamless, intuitive, and human-centered, so that the experience is enhanced rather than needlessly complicated or, more importantly, distracting from the field/court/stage.

"Sustainability will continue to guide our industry and in the next 10 years, we will see the advancement of building systems that are more efficient and lower in embodied carbon.I believe we are approaching the first true mass timber stadium or arena. The designs are out there; we just need to get them built.

"Regardless of the number of solar panels sitting on the roof, or how much supplemental material is mixed into the concrete, a building that operates like a fortress for most of the year is underperforming, both fiscally and sustainably.

"The future of stadium design should be measured not only by the monetization of game day, but by the value these buildings create on ordinary days.

"The next generation of stadiums must maximize return on investment by being profit-focused, technologically advanced, and architecturally ambitious, while also being creative in their openness, usefulness, and how they build a deep connection to the communities they serve."

Future Stadium

This article is part of Future Stadium, our series exploring the growing role of monumental sports buildings in architecture and urbanism around the world.

Dezeen School Shows: a rehabilitative prison in a former mill with crafting and vocational spaces is among the projects from Norwich University of the Arts.

Also featured is a project that explores how Brutalism can complement nature, and a proposal for wellbeing and communal social spaces inside Norwich's city walls.

Norwich University of the Arts

Institution: Architecture and Interior Design Programme
Course: Interior Design
Tutors: Jason Wiggin, Gabriela Jimenez, Gaetano Drago, Teresa Stoppani and Chiara Toscani

School statement:

"The Norwich Interior Design course advances critical spatial practice through collaboration, shared enquiry and material investigation.

"From the shared first-year studio, students work collectively and with local partners, engaging sites across Norwich and the Norfolk coast through mapping, filming, drawing and making.

"Projects explore the interior as an expanded condition shaped by environmental change, social use and spatial memory.

"Working with derelict buildings and underused urban spaces, students develop proposals that support forms of public life and collective occupation, positioning interior design as an evolving field attentive to atmosphere, materiality and lived experience."

(Re)Remembering by Katie Gardiner

"Reimagining the Wymondham graveyard as an active public landscape, this project introduces routes and spaces for walking, gathering and reflection.

"A sequence of glass posts guides visitors toward seven memory gardens, each linking planting with practices of remembrance.

"Paths offer different modes of engagement, including site-specific and symbolic journeys. Enclosed rooms, reflection pools and reused materials establish a spatial language grounded in care and continuity.

"Memory is embedded within both landscape and material. (Re)Remembering frames the graveyard as a shared environment that supports ongoing relationships between people, place and collective histories."

Student: Katie Gardiner
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

City Walls by Mya Frost

"Engaging fragments of Norwich's historic wall, this project repositions them as spaces for movement, occupation and encounter.

"Each site is approached through interventions that respond to its specific conditions, including elevated routes, thresholds and interior insertions.

"Openings and platforms bring visitors into close proximity with the wall's material fabric. Circulation is designed to reveal and conceal views in sequence, shaping perception through movement.

"At key locations, gathering spaces and displays integrate the wall into everyday use. City Walls develops a spatial framework in which heritage becomes part of daily urban experience."

Student: Mya Frost
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Framing Silence by Olivia Stribbling

"Set within Thetford Forest, this project constructs a spatial sequence that engages silence as an embodied condition. A raised walkway compresses movement and light before opening toward water and wider views.

"Branching routes lead to platforms that frame sound, mist and canopy through controlled architectural elements. Material choices, including Corten steel, limestone and timber, respond to the forest's temporal changes.

"Lighting is used sparingly to support atmosphere without overwhelming the site. Framing Silence organises perception through movement, guiding visitors toward focused encounters with sound, landscape and their own presence within the environment."

Student: Olivia Stribbling
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Memoria-Viva: A Living Pavilion of Memory and Becoming by Orlane Mboukou-Etoney

"Developed as a counter-memorial, this project constructs a pavilion that brings forward histories of women in Ancient Rome through spatial experience.

"A sequence of layered environments guides visitors through moments of exposure, reflection and gathering. Architectural devices associated with concealment are reworked into spaces that can be occupied collectively.

"Material, light and sensory elements evoke historical fragments without direct reconstruction. The pavilion is positioned on a site with limited connectivity, activating it through shared use.

"Memoria-Viva frames memory as active and evolving, shaped through movement, occupation and intergenerational presence."

Student: Orlane Mboukou-Etoney
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

The Theatre of Power by Robyn Holmes

"Set within unstable coastal cliffs, this project develops a ritual architecture structured around hierarchy and controlled movement.

"A single processional route compresses the body through narrow corridors and restricted views, guiding visitors toward a central chamber.

"Spatial organisation reinforces roles, with an elevated podium marking authority above a lower field of occupants. Material treatment shifts from light-absorbing surfaces to reflective finishes that intensify focus within the main space.

"An oculus directs light to emphasise position and presence. The Theatre of Power constructs a spatial system in which authority is produced, reinforced and made visible through architecture."

Student: Robyn Holmes
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Bairn by Eve Holmes

"Located within Victor Pasmore's Apollo Pavilion in Peterlee, Bairn proposes a youth centre for 13 to 17-year-olds in a working-class new town in County Durham.

"The title, taken from the local word for 'child', anchors the project in regional identity and everyday language. The centre reactivates the listed structure through contemporary use rather than distant preservation.

"Programme elements are pulled into separate volumes, linked by accessible ramps that act as circulation and social space. Forced perspectives and framed views guide movement and looking.

"Bairn reshapes the pavilion as a place for safety, creativity and shared urban youth culture through art, movement and play."

Student: Eve Holmes
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Zigeden by Harrison Kennedy

"Working within the listed University of East Anglia Ziggurats in Norwich, Zigeden reimagines the Brutalist student accommodation blocks designed by Denys Lasdun around biophilic principles and a shared hub for students and staff.

"The project keeps the concrete forms while testing how Brutalism can sit alongside light, nature and wellbeing. At the centre of the complex, a tall hall expresses biophilic ideas through structure and light rather than heavy planting.

"A suspended perforated steel installation, inspired by (Japanese, literally meaning 'sunlight leaking through trees') filters daylight like a forest canopy, while overlapping landings create layered views and pauses.

"Warm materials, planted columns and fluid interventions thread through the building, treating the existing interior as a living landscape for contemporary student life."

Student: Harrison Kennedy
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Subterranean Futures by Janina Rundberg

"Imagined beneath the former RAF Bardhill Radar Station in North Norfolk, this project develops a subterranean residential community that offers refuge from surface-level instability.

"Families occupy dwelling units cut into the rock, connected to shared spaces such as an underground park, learning rooms, recycling workshops, food production areas and communal baths.

"Levels overlap only where structurally safe, with homes near the surface and collective functions below. Organic forms follow the geology to keep residents psychologically connected to the surrounding earth.

Energy, water and nutrients are drawn from deep heat, filtered rainwater and biomethane systems. Everyday spaces rely on excavated stone and reclaimed materials.

"Subterranean Futures asks how underground living might reshape ideas of community, system and survival."

Student: Janina Rundberg
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

Women's Custodial and Rehabilitation Centre by Izabela Wesolowska

"Developed within St. James Mill in Norwich, this project proposes a rehabilitative Category C women's prison that treats the custodial setting as a place of care, growth and social reintegration.

"New and adapted spaces inside the existing fabric are arranged around routine, education and meaningful daily activity.

"Workshops for crafts, textiles and vocational skills occupy visible, accessible positions, with classrooms and study areas offering calm environments for learning.

"Mother and baby units introduce a domestic-scale setting where early-age relationships can continue. Material choices, daylight and spatial sequencing soften the institutional character to bring together experience and stability beyond the prison."

Student: Izabela Wesolowska
Course: BA (Hons) Interior Design

item.content:encoded:
An external skin of timber louvres filters light and air into the double-height interiors of Waankarn, a restaurant and events space in Thailand designed by local architecture practice Studio Locomotive.

Located in the coastal village of Khao Lak, the space was designed to combine a bar and restaurant for the area's increasing number of tourists, with spaces that can be used by the local community for gatherings and exhibitions.

According to Studio Locomotive, its use of vernacular materials and techniques was a means of allowing visitors to "experience the sensory realities of Southern Thai living", most notably through the breezy walls of louvres made from Ceylon ironwood.

"We approached the context as a living condition, allowing guests to intuitively feel how localised structures breathe and function," Thanart Chanyu, design director at Studio Locomotive, told Dezeen.

"We translated this into an evocative spatial character, managing the tropical climate through strategic architectural apertures, tactile woodwork, and the moisture radiating from earth-bound masonry," he added.

Waankarn's louvre walls wrap two double-height spaces on either side of a wide, stepped concrete corridor, which was designed to double as a space for temporary exhibitions organised by the community.

To the north of this corridor is the main dining room and to the south a smaller bar space, both of which are defined by walls of timber louvres and exposed concrete, skylit ceilings and granite floors.

This simple palette was complemented by the use of repurposed materials, which, according to Studio Locomotive, were a means of creating a "cultural bridge" for visitors less familiar with the area.

In the bar, a countertop was made from a five-centimetre-thick sheet of salvaged industrial steel, which sits in front of a large feature wall created by repurposing a section of local, traditional clay tile roof.

"Over the years of doing fieldwork, we became acquainted with local homeowners. One of these homes was the very last in the area still roofed with traditional clay tiles," Chanyu said.

"When we learned the family was dismantling the roof during our project's construction phase, we asked to carefully preserve the tiles."

"These meaningful pieces can continue their purpose and keep telling the story of the community," he added.

Read:

Tokyo's drinking alleys inform interior of Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio

In the more enclosed eastern side of the building are service spaces such as the kitchen and bathrooms, and a smaller, secondary dining space.

Above, a mezzanine space extends into a walkway that wraps around the double-height spaces below, created to foster a sense of connection between the hospitality and community areas.

This walkway extends up onto Waankarn's roof, where it connects a series of open-air terraces surrounded by concrete planters.

"We interlaced the hospitality programs and the civic paths through a shared network of gallery corridors," explained Chanyu. "This allows both to operate simultaneously without operational friction, yet remain porous enough to allow for interaction."

"Ultimately, we want this architecture to transcend private ownership and play a meaningful role in serving the broader socio-spatial fabric," he concluded.

Previous projects by Studio Locomotive include Tree O'Clock, a community centre for a housing development in Phuket City that is topped by stepped gardens.

The photography is by Pichan Sujaritsatit.

item.content:encoded:
Architect Kenta Hirayama has designed an "unpretentious house" in Tokyo's Setagaya Ward, which features a metal facade and deliberately simple gabled roof.

Called House in Kinuta, the detached home's pared-back design aims to maximise natural light while still providing enough privacy for the young family living in the densely populated area.

"Located in a residential area of Tokyo with a high density, the concept is to create a healthy and comfortable living environment filled with natural light, while managing the views of nearby houses," Hirayama, who leads Kenta Hirayama Architect & Associates, told Dezeen.

The architect chose to add limited but large windows to the 145-square-metre house in Kinuta, Setagaya Ward, which was built using a structural framework of cedar and pine wood.

It was then clad in galvalume steel, which Hirayama describes as "a low-maintenance, cost-effective material that is widely used for residential construction in Japan".

The steel panels were also used to create angular details, such as a small roof above the door to protect from rain, for both decorative and practical effect.

While the steel facade gives the building a contemporary feel, Hirayama kept the house's shape deliberately simple in a nod to the more traditional homes that surround it.

"Around the site, large old pine trees and houses from the good old days are dotted," he said. "I wanted to design an unpretentious house that feels like a natural part of the landscape. For this reason, I designed the appearance with a simple gabled roof."

Read:

Curving metal terrace for potted plants fronts home in Tokyo by HOAA

The ground floor of the house has an atelier with a double-height ceiling, designed specially for the artist client.

Its bedroom is located on the south side of the building, which was set back from the street to create distance from the immediate neighbouring house and add more light.

A bathroom and storage spaces were arranged around the perimeter of the ground floor, while the first floor contains a combined living, dining and kitchen area.

Here, Hirayama added a large bay window and custom-designed lighting with reflectors to illuminate the room.

In contrast to the steely exterior, the inside of the home features plenty of pale natural wood, which was used for the floors and wall panels as well as the furniture.

Hirayama wanted the interior to have a soothing colour palette, using a neutral white hue for the walls and ceilings.

"I tried adjustment by an oil finish to make the interior feel calm, while taking advantage of the colours of the natural materials as much as possible," Hirayama said.

"The structure made of coniferous trees was finished with a light grey oil, which balances the colour with the ash wood of the floor and furniture," he continued. "In addition, the white colour of the walls and ceilings was mixed with just a little grey to balance the colour tone of the space."

Tokyo is known for its innovative residential architecture. Other Tokyo homes recently featured on Dezeen include a house with a curving metal terrace that holds potted plants and a home with an exposed concrete shell that incorporates its furniture.

Dezeen Showroom: surface brand Forbo Flooring's Marmoleum Cocoa flooring makes use of unwanted cocoa shells – an oft-wasted by-product of the cocoa industry.

Marmoleum Cocoa is an evolution of Forbo Flooring's existing Marmoleum range, which is made from up to 98 per cent natural raw materials, including linseed oil, wood flour and jute.

In addition to these, Marmoleum Cocoa contains cocoa shells, which give each of its 16 colourways a distinctive look and feel that the brand describes as "natural yet contemporary".

"By integrating these shells into the flooring, we give new life to an underutilised resource while contributing to a more circular economy," said Forbo Flooring.

The flooring is the result of the brand's collaboration with Dutch-founded social enterprise Kumasi Commodity Innovations. While Forbo Flooring makes use of surplus cocoa shells, Kumasi uses cocoa fruit juice to create its beverages.

"Through its recent partnership with Kumasi, Forbo Flooring sources cocoa shells in a way that directly benefits cocoa farming communities," said the brand.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio MVRDV has designed a flagship store for Chinese fashion brand Urban Revivo in Beijing, China, with a dramatic facade informed by the roof tiles on the city's traditional houses.

Located within Beijing's Sanlitun shopping district, the store sits along the main pedestrian route of the district that connects the south section, known for its young, trendy fashion offerings, and the north section, distinguished by stores for luxury fashion brands.

MVRDV's design for the 4,120-square-metre Urban Revivo aims to respond to the store's location at this intersection by combining a youthful energy with a dramatic facade to capture people's attention.

The result is a facade comprised of an array of suspended aluminium tiles and tubes, with the outward-facing side of each tube engraved with the brand's logo.

The facade also features seven circular openings of various sizes, which were informed by traditional Chinese moon gates and serve as the main entrance to the centre and as window displays.

A series of tiles and tubes protrude along the outlines of the circular openings to create a three-dimensional, wave-like facade design.

Urban Revivo's signature blue colour was applied to the facade and given a dichroic coating that allows the colour to change from purple to blue when viewed from different angles.

"The challenge of this project was to create a space that feels grounded in its surroundings while also reflecting the global aspirations of Urban Revivo", MVRDV founding partner Jacob van Rijs said.

"So we used local references, like Beijing's roof tiles, but combined them with modern techniques to create spaces that evolve with the visitor's experience, from the colour facade to the smallest design details inside," he continued.

The store's interiors feature grey bricks, which were used extensively as a neutral backdrop in a nod to Beijing's traditional Hutong, residential neighbourhoods arranged along narrow alleyways.

MVRDV aimed to create a different atmosphere across each of the four retail floors by changing the shapes of the entrances and using a variety of colours and materials.

Visitors are led through a series of traditional moon gates on the ground floor, consistent with the main entrance.

As they move upstairs, these openings are slowly adjusted to more modern styles – from arched openings on the first floor to rectangles with rounded corners on the second floor and finally to an inverted curve on the top floor.

Read:

MVRDV drapes glass veil around Tiffany & Co flagship in Beijing

Reflective surface and bright blue furniture on the first floor create a bold and youthful feeling, while darker and more refined materials define the second floor, which targets more mature customers.

Velvet and cobalt blue upholstery on the top floor aim to create an intimate ambience for private shopping.

Additionally, six Bold Rooms were designed to display special collections throughout the store.

These include the Soft Room, enclosed by upholstered cushions on the walls; the Playful Room, filled with display blocks made from recycled fabric; the Urban Room with a reflective surface and the Daring Room, which uses wooden boxes for product display.

The Unexpected Room is lined with fabric curtains, which change in colour and material to match the collection it will present, while the Avant Garde Room, positioned along the two atriums of the building, presents products in glass cases.

"From a facade inspired by Beijing roof tiles and a modern interpretation of traditional arches to contemporary materials, the design combines these two seemingly opposing impulses into one immersive retail environment," said MVRDV.

"The project reflects both the cosmopolitan global outlook of Urban Revivo and a connection to the local architectural context of the Chinese capital," it added.

Beijing's Sanlitun shopping district has become a playground for architects to experiment with bold facade design for fashion labels.

MVRDV also recently completed a facade with a curving glass veil for a Tiffany & Co flagship store here, while Japanese studio Jun Aoki & Associates designed a Louis Vuitton flagship with a translucent and fluid form.

item.content:encoded:
Bio-designer Lucia Giron has worked with the University of Cambridge's Department of Biochemistry to develop prototypes of an algae-based battery alternative, which harnesses the power of photosynthesis for electricity.

The University of Cambridge is one of the pioneers of biophotovoltaics, which work like biological solar panels, converting light into electrical current through the natural processes of living microorganisms.

In the Cambridge team's "biocells", the microorganisms are cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, and the electricity is generated continuously as they carry out photosynthesis, taking energy from sunlight and feeding on carbon dioxide to grow.

The researchers believe these low-powered biocells could one day eliminate the need for the small chemical batteries that power many everyday devices like remote controls and smoke alarms, causing ecological damage through their mining and disposal.

"Our technology could replace millions of small disposable batteries with a much cleaner source of energy – that's a huge environmental benefit and a really exciting prospect," said University of Cambridge professor Chris Howe.

Howe and his team have been working with Giron, a 2023 graduate of the Biodesign masters at London school Central Saint Martins, for the last two and a half years. Along with engineer Lifu Tan, she has been helping the scientists turn their research into prototypes that demonstrate the technology in action.

Their creations include a demonstrator cell – which presents the technology in a compact, attractive and recognisable package – as well as a clock radio and a temperature sensor powered by biophotovoltaic (BPV) panels.

The demonstrator cell was designed to communicate what biophotovoltaics are to a new audience, Giron told Dezeen, while catering to the needs of the algae.

"One of the interesting tensions with designing a biocell is that you're trying to create something that behaves like a piece of technology while also accommodating a living organism – in other words, designing the conditions for the organism to interact with the device," she said.

Within this context, the biocell's contained algae is exposed within a transparent casing, which serves a dual functional and aesthetic purpose.

"The algae need access to light in order to photosynthesise," said Giron. "The transparency [also] allows people to see the living system inside, which hopefully creates a sense of curiosity and connection with the process happening within the cell."

A special semi-permeable membrane allows gas exchange while preventing evaporation, and the electrode inside has a filamentous structure that provides a textured surface for the algae to integrate with, allowing the biological and electrical parts of the system to interact more closely.

The decorative leaf-vein design on the front plate serves as an easily recognisable symbol of photosynthesis. This front plate can be removed and the system disassembled so its components can be reused or recycled.

The algae are not harmed in the creation or use of the cell and keep producing electricity for the duration of their lives. In the Cambridge scientists' lab, this is six years and counting.

This is also the case in the two BPV panels: a disc-shaped one that Giron and the team designed to plug into a temperature sensor, and a rectangular slab that slots into the top of a clock radio. These show how the technology might exist in everyday life.

Currently, the BPV panels are much larger than standard disposable batteries, matching or even exceeding the size of the demonstrator devices they power. But they will likely get smaller as the scientists commercialise their technology through their new spin-out company, e-Pho.

"I think there are probably two directions this technology could move in," said Giron. "There is definitely potential for the systems to become more compact as we continue to understand and optimise them, but I also think there's something interesting about not hiding the technology away."

"Biocells rely on a living process, so they need access to light (whether that's sunlight or indoor light), which means they may always have a slightly different relationship to the spaces they inhabit," she continued.

"Many of the energy technologies we interact with every day are designed to be invisible, but with biocells, part of the opportunity is that they make energy production more visible and create a relationship between people and the living systems generating it."

Size and portability will be crucial for some applications, but for contexts like education, public spaces and architecture, "helping people understand how [energy] is produced could actually be part of its value", Giron argued.

Other recent appearances of cyanobacteria in design include the Canadian pavilion of the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, where the microorganisms coated a lattice structure to sequester carbon, and in Studio Swine's Invisible Worlds sculpture, which celebrated their status as the world's first oxygen-producing photosynthesizers.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: Spanish brand Cosentino merges beauty, performance and sustainability with its latest mineral surface material, Éclos, designed to be free of crystalline silica and as elegant as natural stone.

Made using Cosentino's most advanced methods and decoration techniques, Éclos is a next-generation engineered stone with rich veining and patterning.

Thanks to the brand's proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, this patterning runs through the slab, creating a natural and sophisticated aesthetic that is unbroken at the edges.

The company describes Éclos as an entirely new category of material, which it calls an "inlayered mineral surface". The designs are constructed in layers using advanced robotic engineering, giving them their remarkable depth and realism.

As well as visual impact, Éclos is designed for safety and sustainability, Cosentino explained. It has a zero crystalline silica formula that is favourable for installers during cutting, and a high percentage of recycled mineral content of close to 90 per cent for some colour options.

Éclos joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surfaces from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

According to Cosentino, the development of Éclos involved 50 specialised researchers, more than 28,000 hours of research and over 1,500 hours of testing, reflecting the company's commitment to environmental protection and fabricator safety.

"Since our founding, we have been committed to leading innovation rather than following trends, just as we did with Dekton and most recently with Hybriq+ technology for Silestone," said Cosentino Group CEO Pilar Cosentino.

"Éclos involves a new turning point for our industry, an evolution that responds to real market needs and anticipates the future."

Éclos is suitable for both residential and commercial environments, and can be used on countertops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces, bringing an elevated look and enjoyable tactility to every space it touches.

The first Éclos collection – Eclectic Veins – brings together 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, by way of warm, earthy and biscuity bases.

Among the standouts is Legnd, a seductive golden brown shot through with spidery dark veins, giving a romantic and mystical feel, and Tajnar, a far-from-boring beige with dense, feathered patterning.

All of the colours in the collection incorporate a minimum of 50 per cent recycled materials, while some incorporate up to 88 per cent recycled content.

The material is durable, withstands everyday scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain. It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 Degrees Celsius, including direct contact with cookware immediately after use, making it highly practical for kitchens.

Headquartered in Spain, Cosentino is a global family-owned business with operations in more than 120 countries.

It utilises 100 per cent renewable energy and 99 per cent recycled water in its factories, helping to lower the environmental footprint of its products.

Dezeen School Shows: a renewable energy centre converting seaweed and flying-fish waste into biogas is among the projects from Norwich University of the Arts.

Also featured is a subterranean architectural project for animals and a wildlife rehabilitation centre made from reclaimed sea defence timber.

Norwich University of the Arts

Institution: Architecture and Interior Design Programme
Course: Architecture BA (Hons) and Architecture MArch
Tutors: Claudia Morgado, William Burgess, William Hailiang Chen, Tony Clelford, Sarah de Villiers, Gaetano Drago, Iuliana Gavril, February Phillips, Teresa Stoppani, George Themistokleous and Romanos Tsomos

School statement:

"The Norwich Architecture programme advances forms of critical spatial practice at a time of environmental pressure and social change.

"Students work in collaboration with local partners, industries and communities, developing projects through shared enquiry, experimental making and spatial storytelling.

"Grounded in East Anglia's coastal landscapes and heritage contexts, undergraduate studios treat the region as a testing ground where shifting shorelines, material histories and environmental change make global issues legible and open to design investigation.

"The postgraduate studio takes a wider view and engages directly with the global dimension of like issues, exploring the fragility, adaptability and local knowledge of remote sites affected by the climate crisis and related socio-economic transformations.

"From the shared first-year studio to postgraduate study, the work develops into research-led proposals that are socially embedded and attentive to environmental responsibility, collective forms of practice and the consequences of material decisions."

Exoskeletal Ecologies by Ben Ludlam

"Situated on the coastline of Orford, this project explores architecture as an exoskeletal ecology where human, animal and industrial systems become physically entangled.

"Cycles of extraction, consumption and transformation are traced through the figure of the crab, and a harvesting machine that transports live catch into a visible processing environment. Visitors dine alongside machinery, confronting production directly.

"Movement through compressed tunnels, suspended walkways and submerged thresholds destabilises the body after consumption. Restricting passages imposes crawling and sideways movements on the human inhabitants.

"Exoskeletal Ecologies establishes a closed loop where waste is reused as bait within a continuous system."

Student: Ben Ludlam
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: ben.ludlam04[at]gmail.com

An Archival Double by Louie Paterson Dean

"This project proposes an archive for the fragile landscape of Orford Ness. Drawing from Anthony Vidler's Dark Space and W.G. Sebald's The Rings of Saturn, the scheme explores the relationship between environmental change and how it is captured through analogue photography.

"Camera obscuras distributed across the site capture views determined not by human intention but by wind and changeable landscape conditions.

"These images are transported, developed, stored and projected by a community of archivists whose labour sustains the archive.

"Inspired by Louis Kahn's distinction between 'servant' and 'served' spaces, the architecture initially privileges the visitor, concealing the archivists behind mirrored boundaries.

"However, in the archive storage chamber, spatial ambiguity destabilises this hierarchy. As time passes, weathered decay triggers accidental failures that disrupt the analogue apparatus.

"Gradually, the site itself assumes authorship over the archive, transforming the architecture into a 'way of seeing' through which environmental degradation overtakes the production of the image, allowing the site to determine what can be seen."

Student: Louie Paterson Dean
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: louiepatersondean[at]gmail.com

Archiving War: Forensic Investigation of Orfordness by Anastasiia Milenko

"Drawing on forensic architecture as both method and framework, this project investigates Orford Ness as a site shaped by histories of violence.

"It proposes an archive and research centre for collecting evidence, testimony and spatial analysis related to contemporary conflict.

"The archive is conceived as open and evolving, allowing contributions from affected communities while resisting centralised control.

"Work operates across the site's military past and current global conditions. Archiving War: Forensic Investigation of Orfordness positions architecture as a tool for inquiry, supporting the organisation and circulation of knowledge that informs public understanding and accountability."

Student: Anastasiia Milenko
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: vivo.vivace.2[at]gmail.com

Selkie by Jakob Rode-Christoffersen

"Embedded within a shingle landscape, this project develops a subterranean architecture shaped by compression, darkness and controlled light.

"Spaces are stripped of comfort, focusing on bodily experience through narrow tunnels, low chambers and vertical shafts of light.

"A seal rehabilitation centre sits alongside human inhabitation, establishing proximity between species and shared conditions of recovery.

"Activities such as foraging, eating and rest structure occupation, while communal and individual spaces are carefully differentiated.

"Sunken courtyards reconnect interior and surface environments. Selkie uses the seal as a model for inhabiting space through embodied, environmental and cyclical relations."

Student: Jakob Rode-Christoffersen
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: jakobl.rc[at]gmail.com

A Second Life: Reclaiming Timber, Rebuilding Habitat by Jade Luxwolda

"Situated within a coastal landscape, this project develops an architecture that supports environmental regeneration, wildlife care, and public engagement.

"A rehabilitation centre is combined with education and accommodation, allowing ecological processes to be observed and understood.

"The design is grounded in circular construction, using reclaimed harbour and sea defence timber as its primary material.

"This extends material lifespans while reducing environmental impact. Spaces are arranged to protect sensitive habitats while enabling access.

"Elevated walkways and sheltered structures mediate between visitors and landscape. A Second Life: Reclaiming Timber, Rebuilding Habitat establishes a material and ecological continuity."

Student: Jade Luxwolda
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture

Mediated Optical Fields by Martine Qvernstrøm

"Using photography as an optical system, this project examines perception as an embodied and spatial condition. Orford Ness is engaged as both subject and medium through a series of constructed viewing environments.

"The proposal centres on the Black Beacon, an immersive chamber informed by the camera obscura, where light, reflection and inversion reframe the surrounding landscape.

"Visitors move through calibrated gradients of darkness and illumination that heighten awareness of bodily presence.

"Philosophical ideas of perception inform the work, positioning vision as contingent and constructed. Mediated Optical Fields develops architecture as a device for sensing and interpreting space."

Student: Martine Qvernstrøm
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: martineqve[at]gmail.com

Oxidation of a Destructive Landscape by Tom Whitmore

"Addressing contamination at Orford Ness, this project proposes a phytoremediation strategy that uses plant systems to absorb and transform pollutants.

"Former military structures are adapted into testing environments where selected species interact with contaminated soil and material residues.

"Drawing on the concept of the parasitic chain, new ecological agents alter site conditions while generating further outputs.

"Over time, metal is metabolised into plant growth, producing a shifting and productive landscape. Oxidation of a Destructive Landscape frames remediation as an ongoing ecological process embedded within material cycles and site histories."

Student: Tom Whitmore
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: twhitterz[at]icloud.com

Seasonal Assemblage by Megi Muslia

"Located within the marshlands of Orford Ness, this project develops architecture as a system shaped by seasonal growth, decay and repair.

"Drawing on the life cycle of the common reed, it proposes a settlement that evolves with its environment.

"Reed is used as a material skin that is harvested, assembled and replaced over time, linking construction with maintenance and occupation. Programme shifts throughout the year, supporting cycles of harvesting, storage and communal activity.

"Informed by root networks and microbial systems, Seasonal Assemblage frames architecture as an ongoing interaction between human and non-human processes within a changing landscape."

Student: Megi Muslia
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: megimuslia[at]gmail.com

The Naust at The Ness by Emma Johansen

"Located along the River Ore, this project establishes a workshop centred on boatbuilding as a spatial and cultural practice.

"Timber construction and assembly define both the building and the activities within it, linking material process with architectural form.

"The workshop supports making, teaching and community use through a series of connected spaces that allow knowledge to circulate.

"Tidal conditions shape the rhythms of occupation and construction. Craft is made visible through the organisation of structure and programme.

"The Naust at The Ness positions the workshop as a collective environment grounded in material practice and shared learning."

Student: Emma Johansen
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: emmasofiejoh[at]gmail.com

Into and Out of Orchid Island by Sam Joy

"Grounded in Tao indigenous knowledge, this project examines socio-ecological systems structured through seasonal fishing, intergenerational exchange and reciprocal spatial relations with the ocean.

"It reorients imposed nuclear and gasoline infrastructures through a community-scaled hybrid structure that harvests seaweed and flying-fish waste, digesting them into biogas while housing communal allocation, cooking and material-testing spaces in a semi-subterranean timber, bamboo and seaweed-based envelope.

"Located in Imourod, Orchid Island, the scheme aligns with routes toward the Batanes archipelago to reassert archipelagic relations and stages the voyage south again, repositioning ocean relations as the basis for Tao cultural transmission, community energy autonomy and ongoing material experimentation within local circularities."

Student: Sam Joy
Course: BA (Hons) Architecture
Email: sam-Joy[at]outlook.com

Sponge Logic Living by Maria Houlden Fernandez

"Located within the coastal landscape of Heybridge, Essex, England, the project explores how architecture can support living with water through spatial systems that hold, filter and modulate changing conditions.

"Water is treated as an active presence across the site, shaping courtyards, walkways and floodable edges that respond to tidal and climatic variation.

"Existing hydrological features, including former gravel pits, inform a porous ground condition that absorbs and slowly releases water over time, operating as a sponge-like infrastructural field.

"Wetland habitats support shared occupation with species such as the water vole, a protected semi-aquatic rodent. Sponge Logic Living develops a residential prototype that aligns domestic space with ecological and hydrological cycles."

Student: Maria Houlden Fernandez
Course: MArch
